bio.en: Paul Adams is Chief Product Officer at Intercom, a role he has held for over ten years, after previously serving as global head of brand design at Facebook, a user researcher at Google, and a product designer at Dyson.
bio.zh: Paul Adams 是 Intercom 的首席产品官（CPO），担任该职务已超过十年，此前曾任 Facebook 全球品牌设计负责人、Google 用户研究员，以及 Dyson 产品设计师。

summary.en: Paul shares candid stories of professional failure - including freezing on stage at Cannes - and argues that failure is essential experience for product leaders. He goes deep on Intercom's all-in embrace of AI, explaining why leaders must move from fear and noise to actively trying the technology, and draws parallels to the mobile shift a decade ago. The episode blends personal vulnerability with sharp advice on building craft-focused, AI-native products.
summary.zh: Paul 坦诚分享了自己职业中的失败经历——包括在戛纳演讲时当众卡壳——并主张失败是产品领导者必不可少的历练。他深入讲解了 Intercom 全面拥抱 AI 的历程，解释领导者为何必须从恐惧与喧嚣转向真正动手尝试这项技术，并与十年前的移动化浪潮作了类比。本期将个人的脆弱坦诚与关于打造注重工艺、AI 原生产品的犀利建议结合在一起。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: This is a meteor coming towards you. This is going to radically transform society. And I think if people don't explore AI properly, it will leave them behind. I'd start with the thing your product does. "What's the core premise behind it? Why do people use it? What problem does it solve for them?" That kind of thing. So, go back to basics. And then ask, "Can AI do that?" And for a lot, the answer is going to be, "Yes, it can." For some it might be, "It can partially do it." And then, maybe for others, "It can't do that, at least not yet." And then, for some of it'll be replacement, AI would replace, it'll just do it. And, in other places, it'll be augmentation. It'll augment. It'll help people. But yeah, I think that you've got to match your product, and what AI can do, and what it will be able to do, and then ask yourself, "Okay, what are we going to do?"
turns.zh: 这是一颗正朝你飞来的流星。它将彻底改变社会。我认为，如果人们不充分探索人工智能（AI），将会被时代淘汰。我建议先审视你们的产品核心理念："它的核心假设是什么？人们为何会使用它？它为用户解决了哪些问题？"诸如此类的问题。回归基础，再反问："AI能做到这些吗？"对许多产品而言，答案会是"能"；对某些产品，答案可能是"部分能"；而对其他产品，答案则会是"至少目前还做不到"。有些场景下，AI会完全取代现有功能；在另一些场景下，它会进行辅助增强，帮助人类完成任务。但归根结底，关键在于将产品与AI的现有能力和未来发展潜力相结合，然后问自己："接下来我们该怎么做？"

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. Nice to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢，莱尼。很高兴能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's nice to have you here. I've heard so many good things about you from so many different people, so I'm really happy that we're finally doing this. Also, you have an Irish accent, which is always a boost for ratings in my experience, so thank you for bringing that with you here.
turns.zh: 很高兴你能来这里。我听过很多人对你的赞誉，所以很高兴我们终于能见面了。还有，你带有爱尔兰口音，这在我的经验中总是能提升收视率的，感谢你带来了这个特色。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, that's nice to hear.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真让人欣慰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wanted to start with a couple stories. So the first is your story of giving a keynote at Cannes. Can you share what happened there?
turns.zh: 我想先分享几个故事。第一个是关于你在戛纳做主题演讲的。能讲讲当时的情况吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, some things that happened in work are very memorable at the time and they don't really scar you. This goes in the book that have scarred for life. Yeah, it's good. Long story short, I was at Facebook just over a decade ago. Loved it at the time. I think it was a great place to be at the time. And, basically San Francisco, I did a lot of talks for Facebook internally and externally. Facebook had a keynote slot, always had a keynote slot at Cannes, the world's biggest advertising festival. And, the year prior, Zuck had been interviewed. He was the speaker, he'd been interviewed. He'd gotten a hard time on privacy. It didn't go well as well as they'd hoped. (00:05:14): So, the next year they asked me to do it. Maybe it was the Irish accent that made the offer come my way. And, yeah, I got out and spun a stage, the world's biggest advertising stage. And, I'd say, I was three, four minutes into the talk, a very similar talk when I'd given lots of times. And, I just froze. I couldn't remember what I was supposed to say. It was the first ever time in my life I'd rehearsed the talk word for word. Usually, I have talking points, and things get mixed around, and it's informal. This was media trained, "Do not say the wrong thing." Kind of talk. And I just could not remember what to say. I had some version of a panic attack, walked off-stage, I was still mic'd up, cursed. Everyone started laughing. I was like, "Geez, are they laughing at me? Oh my God, this is..." (00:06:06): But, I managed to turn it around, I walked back out. I'd been disarmed internally in my head. And, the most of it went well. And I was famous that night. Out in Cannes afterwards on whatever the sea front, it's just like rose everywhere. And yeah, I was famous and infamous for my performance.
turns.zh: 是啊，有些工作中的经历当时觉得很难忘，但其实并不会给你留下深深的阴影。这才算是真正刻骨铭心的经历。简而言之，大约十多年前我在Facebook工作。当时很喜欢那里，觉得那是个很棒的工作环境。基本上，当时我在旧金山为Facebook内部和外部做了很多演讲。Facebook在戛纳这个全球最大的广告节上一直有主题演讲的席位。前一年，扎克伯格接受采访时，作为演讲嘉宾，在隐私问题上被问得很难堪，效果并不理想。（00:05:14）所以第二年他们邀请我上台。也许是爱尔兰口音帮我赢得了这个机会。是啊，我走上世界最大的广告舞台，开始了三四分钟的演讲，内容和之前很多次差不多。结果我完全僵住了，忘了该说什么。这是我人生中第一次逐字逐句地排练演讲。通常我只是准备几个要点，然后随意发挥。但这次是经过媒体训练的，“不能说错话”之类的。结果我完全记不清该说什么了。我几乎是恐慌发作，走下舞台时还戴着麦克风，咒骂个不停。所有人都笑了。我当时想：“天哪，他们是在笑我吗？哦，天哪，这太……”（00:06:06）不过我还是调整了过来，重新走上舞台。当时我内心已经崩溃了。但大部分情况都还顺利。那晚我在戛纳海滨到处走，备受关注。是啊，我因为这次表现既出名又出丑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you lived the worst nightmare that everybody has when they're thinking about giving a talk. And, I think what's interesting is you survived. And, I think that's a really interesting lesson is you could freeze in front of thousands of people, walk off-stage, and then it works out okay.
turns.zh: 我觉得你经历了每个人做演讲时最可怕的噩梦。更有趣的是你挺过来了。我觉得这是一个很有启发的教训——即使面对数千人的观众，你可能会紧张到走下舞台，但最终结果还不错。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And it all happened organically, I guess, or very naturally. But yeah, ever since then, every time I walk out onto a conference talk stage, still today, I have this tiny doubt in the back of my head. It's never happened since. But yeah, I think you have to go with it with these things, when life throws you these, whatever, curveballs you have got to adapt and it's not that big a deal. None of these things are that big a deal, at the end of the day. You move on and live and learn. So yeah, but I still hope it doesn't happen again.
turns.zh: 是啊。这整个过程都是自然而然的。但从那以后，每次走上会议演讲台，我心里总会有那么一丝不安。不过这种情况再没发生过。但是，我觉得遇到这种事，就顺其自然吧。生活总会抛给你各种难题，你得随机应变，事情其实没那么严重。说到底，这些都不是什么大事。继续前进，生活，学习。是啊，但我还是希望这种情况别再发生了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also hate public speaking and I always fear this is exactly what's going to happen to me. And so, I think this is nice to hear, that even when the worst possible thing basically happens, things can survive.
turns.zh: 我也讨厌公开演讲，总担心自己会遇到这种情况。所以，听到你说即便发生了最糟糕的情况，事情依然能挺过去，这真令人欣慰。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: You can turn it around. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你可以转念一想。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A second area I wanted to hear from is your time at Google. And, there's a couple products you worked on at Google. Both of them were not what you'd call big successes. And then, there's a transition to Facebook, which was also messy. Can you just share a couple stories from that time?
turns.zh: 接下来我想听听你在谷歌的经历。你在谷歌参与过几个产品项目，但都不算特别成功。然后你转投Facebook，这段过渡期也相当波折。你能分享一下那段时期的几个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. Similar to the walking on stage thing, you live and learn. And, I was at Google for four years now and I was at Facebook for two and a half years or so. And, in both of those companies, this is at the height of... The social tech wave was at its peak. Google were very afraid of the existential threat posed by Facebook. Facebook were very confident they could pull off some new social advertising unit that would be an AdWords or something like that, that would destroy Google's revenue, eat them from the inside out. And so, being there at the time was fascinating and moving to the new companies. At Google, I worked on a lot of failed social projects, like you mentioned. Google Buzz, Google Ventilator, Google Plus. I think, a lot of the motivation for those projects came from a place of fear. It didn't come from a place of, "Let's make a great product for people. Let's really understand the things people struggle with when communicating with family and friends. Let's really, really try and create something wonderful." It came from a place of fear. (00:08:47): And so, during those times, I learned I think how not to lead in places. And by the way, I should say, at the time in Google, there was other things happening that were amazing, like Google were building Google Maps, an incredible product. One of my favorite products. I think one of the best products ever made. They were building Android. I was in the mobile team and the mobile apps team at the time, the Android came out. So, they can make an incredibly good product. So, I just happened to be in the social side, which wasn't as good. And, yeah, Google Buzz is a privacy disaster, and Google Plus is similar. (00:09:24): And so, halfway through I'd published research about groups and I'd done a ton of research. An interesting side note there is, at the time, I was working in the UX team as a researcher, I was been asked to do a lot of tactical research, like usability study type stuff, like can people use these products? And, I ended up doing a lot of formative research as well in the same session. So, I'd say to the team, "Hey, I'll do the research. I'll answer your questions. But also, I'm going to do this other thing, and I'm going to take 20 minutes doing that." And so, what we used to do is, what I used to do with people was map out their social network, all the people in it, their family, their friends, how they communicate. We'd map on all the channels, we'd talk about what worked well, what didn't. And, we did this with dozens and dozens of people over the course of maybe 18 months. And the same pattern emerged every single time, which was, people need way better ways to communicate with small groups of family and friends. (00:10:17): And I look back now and go like, "WhatsApp." Or it may be iMessage if everyone's on Apple. But, really obvious in hindsight. But at the time, not obvious. And so, we tried to build a product around that called Google Plus. But, again, it came from the wrong place. And so, halfway through, the research that I've done, all this research had been made public through a conference talk. And, Facebook noticed, got in touch, one thing led to another, and I left and joined Facebook, which was an amazing thing for me, personally. (00:10:51): Facebook was an amazing place at the time and exciting. And they were trying to do things for the other reasons, the good reasons. "Okay, let's build an amazing product for people."
turns.zh:
是啊。这和上台演讲类似，经验都是慢慢积累的。我在谷歌待了四年，在Facebook待了两年半左右。这两家公司正值社交科技浪潮的高峰期。谷歌当时非常担忧Facebook带来的生存威胁，而Facebook则自信能推出类似AdWords的社交广告单元，从而彻底击垮谷歌的营收。身处其中的经历既令人着迷，又充满挑战。在谷歌，我参与过许多失败的社交项目，比如Google Buzz、Google Ventilator和Google Plus。我认为这些项目的动机大多源于恐惧感——而非“为用户创造优质产品”，或者真正理解亲友沟通时面临的痛点，而是出于防御心理。

（00:08:47）在那段时期，我学到了如何避免在错误的方向上领导团队。顺便说一句，谷歌当时也有许多惊艳的进展，比如打造了令人惊叹的地图产品（我最爱的产品之一）和安卓系统。我当时在移动团队，安卓刚问世时我就在那儿。他们确实能打造出优秀的产品，但我在社交领域的经历却不尽如人意。Google Buzz的隐私灾难和Google Plus的平庸表现都是例证。

（00:09:24）中途，我发表了关于群组的研究报告，积累了大量研究数据。有趣的是，当时我在用户体验团队担任研究员，被要求做大量实用研究，比如可用性测试。但我最终在同一时段进行了形成性研究。我对团队说：“我会完成你们的需求，但我还要做另一件事，每次用20分钟。”我们会绘制用户的社交网络图，标注亲友关系，分析沟通痛点。在18个月里，数十人参与了研究，每次结果都惊人地相似——人们需要更高效的亲友小群沟通工具。

（00:10:17）回首往事，我会感叹：“这不就是WhatsApp吗？”或者如果大家用苹果设备，可能就是iMessage。但事后看来再明显不过，但当时却被忽视了。于是我们开发了Google Plus，但方向又错了。中途，我完成的研究成果通过会议报告公之于众，Facebook注意到后，经过沟通，我离开谷歌加入了Facebook，这对我个人来说是个绝佳的转机。

（00:10:51）当时Facebook令人惊叹且充满活力，他们的动机是正向的：“让我们为用户创造出色的产品。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this was during Google Plus being built, you basically shifted.
turns.zh: 这是在Google+正在开发期间，你基本上是被调离了。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, midway, I'm stressed to even tell you about it. The project hadn't been launched, it was still under wraps. It was highly confidential. Google had done a lot of things at the time that were the first for them. I don't know if they've done them since. But things like, everyone worked in Google Plus was sent to a different building. That building had a different key card. If you didn't work in Google Plus you could not get in. All sorts of counter-cultural things at the time. And, as a result, there was a lot of antagonism internally for Google Plus. And so, when I left in the middle of the project, leaving with all of the plans in my head to the enemy, some people saw me as a traitor, understandably. Other people thought I was enlightened, too fancy you talked to. But it was the right thing for me to do. But at the time, it was a hard thing to do.
turns.zh: 是的，中途，我甚至都不敢跟你细说。那个项目还没上线，还处于保密阶段。高度机密。当时Google做了很多对他们来说是第一次尝试的事。我不知道他们之后有没有再做过。比如，所有参与Google+项目的人都被调到了另一栋楼。那栋楼有不同的门禁卡。不在Google+部门的人进不去。当时各种反主流的做法。结果，Google+内部有很多反对的声音。所以，当我在项目中途离开时，带着所有设计图投奔竞争对手，有些人觉得我叛变了，这也可以理解。也有人觉得我高明，觉得我太自命不凡了。但对我来说，这是正确的选择。不过当时，这确实很难做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know there's also a lot of scrutiny in what you took with you and the process.
turns.zh: 我知道你带走的东西和整个过程也受到了很多审查。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, when I left, Google assumed that I was one of the spies. I was quarantined. I told them I was leaving. They forensically analyzed my laptop, all sorts of stuff like that. So, it was pretty intense. Looking back, I can understand why that happened. But the root cause for me is that the project has been run from a place of competitive fear, which I don't think leads to good things.
turns.zh: 是的，我离开时，Google怀疑我是个间谍。他们对我进行隔离审查。我告诉他们我要走了，他们还对我的笔记本电脑进行取证分析，各种检查。当时真的很紧张。现在回想起来，我能理解他们为什么那么做。但根本原因是，这个项目从一开始就带着竞争恐惧的心态去运作的，我觉得这注定不会有好结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one of the themes through the stories you just shared is, let's say, failure is... I don't want to make it that harsh, but just things not working out. And, I'm curious as a product leader, how important you think that is for people to go through, if you think that's something that is almost a good thing? And, I guess just is there anything there that you find helpful as a coach, as a mentor, as two people that are trying to become basically you?
turns.zh: 所以你刚刚分享的故事中，有一个主题就是，失败就是……我不想说得太绝对，但就是事情没有成功。我很好奇，作为产品负责人，您认为人们经历失败有多重要？您是否认为这几乎是件好事？我猜，作为教练、导师，或者是两个正在努力成为您那样的人的人，有没有什么经验能对他们有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Very, very. It still is. It still is. I've personally failed so many times. There are two stories and the Google one is long deep tentacles. They're two stories. I failed a ton of times. I remember, when I was at Facebook I was very happy. And, I knew Eoghan and Des, the co-founders of Intercom. And, they were trying to persuade me to join Intercom. We were like, it was a 10-person company at the time. But, Eoghan said something to me at that time which has stuck with me ever since. He said, "At Facebook, you can design the product. But at Intercom, you can design the company." And, that was extremely appealing to me, a great pitch. He's like, "Just design the company with us that you want to work in." (00:13:41): And so, part of that was a company that embraces failure, that says it's okay to try things. I'm a big believer in big bets, high risk, high reward. I don't get as excited about incremental things. No, I haven't said that. There's of course a place for that too, especially as companies get bigger. But, I get excited about big bets. And if you make big bets, you're going to get a lot of it wrong. So a lot of the principles that we built here at Intercom are in building software. (00:14:09): We have a principle called Ship to Learn. And, we've actually changed it since. It's over on the wall here. Ship fast, ship early, ship often is what it says now. You say Ship to Learn. Ship fast, ship early, ship often. So, in that idea is the idea of failure. It's not going to go right. And, it's going to go wrong more often than not. But if you ship early, and fast, and learn fast, you can change fast, and you can improve fast. And, that's the culture that we, as much as possible, try to embrace and teach people. But it's much easier said than done.
turns.zh: 是的，非常，非常。现在依然如此。我个人失败过很多次。这里有两个故事，谷歌那段经历太过复杂。总之，这两个故事都让我深刻领悟到失败的价值。记得我在Facebook的时候，心情特别愉悦。当时我认识了Intercom的联合创始人Eoghan和Des，他们当时正极力劝我加入Intercom。那时Intercom还只有10个人，但Eoghan当时对我说的一句话让我刻骨铭心。他说：“在Facebook，你可以设计产品；但在Intercom，你可以设计公司。”这句话对我极具吸引力，是个绝佳的招募策略。他说：“和我们一起设计你理想中的公司。”（00:13:41）Intercom的文化之一就是鼓励拥抱失败，允许尝试新事物。我坚信大胆尝试、高风险高回报的理念。对于渐进式改进，我并不感冒。当然，公司发展到一定规模后，也需要关注这些。但我更热衷于大胆尝试。若想大胆尝试，就难免会犯很多错误。因此，Intercom构建软件的核心原则之一是“快速迭代，快速学习”。（00:14:09）我们后来对这条原则进行了调整。墙上现在写着：“快速发布，快速迭代，快速学习。”最初的版本是“快速迭代，快速学习”。但现在我们更强调“快速发布，快速迭代，快速学习”。其核心理念就是承认失败不可避免，错误常会发生。但通过快速发布、快速迭代和快速学习，就能快速调整和改进。这正是我们尽可能推行并教导团队的文化。但说起来容易做起来难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Especially when you're in the moment like, "God dammit. Everything's going to fall apart. I really messed this one up."
turns.zh: 是啊。当你身处其中，比如：“天哪，一切都要崩盘了。我这次真的搞砸了。”

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And there's a trade-off with quality that people really struggle with. We've high standards of ourselves. A lot of Intercom comes from a design founder background. We value the craft a lot. We never want to be embarrassed by what we ship. So there's a real tension there, a real trade-off, where people have these high standards, which we encourage. We encourage them to ship fast, and learn, and make mistakes. It's a constant tension that we're navigating.
turns.zh: 是的。人们在质量与速度之间常常难以平衡。我们对自己要求很高。在Intercom，许多人都有设计师出身的背景，我们非常重视工艺。我们绝不希望发布的产品令自己难堪。所以这存在着真正的矛盾，真正的权衡。一方面，我们鼓励人们追求高标准；另一方面，我们又希望他们快速发布、快速学习、快速改进。这是我们一直在应对的持续张力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of taking big bets and going all in, I know there's been a huge shift at Intercom to move towards AI and embrace AI. And so, maybe just to start broadly, I'm curious just what are some of your broader insights or surprises so far in how you've thought about AI and how you think AI will integrate into product and product strategy?
turns.zh: 说到大胆尝试和全力以赴，我知道Intercom在转向AI和拥抱AI方面有了巨大转变。那么，先从宏观层面说起，我很好奇到目前为止，你们对AI的思考有何更广泛的见解或惊喜？AI将如何融入产品和产品战略？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: What day that ChatGPT launch? November 29th, I think, last year. Ever since that day, I literally wake up every day thinking about AI pretty much. And, I read as much as possible and still feel like I'm way behind in it. I think, for me, when I talk to you about AI, people typically fall into one of two camps. You're either all in, really truly all in. This is a meteor coming towards you. This is bigger than mobile as a technology shift, as big as the internet. Maybe it's bigger than the internet itself as a technology shift, the way it'll shape society. So I'm all in. I've gone over the hill or whatever. I'm over the other side. And so, there's people in that camp. (00:16:23): And then, I think there's people in another camp, which is, "I've heard this before. It's hype. Last year was crypto. It was Web3. None of those things worked out. There was the metaverse." So, there's definitely I think a lot of skepticism or maybe cynicism around it. And I don't understand why. The other things didn't really pan out. The metaverse is coming back. And, I'm trying to remember, there's the law where you have the hype, and then the trough of disillusionment, and then you come out the other side.
turns.zh: ChatGPT 是什么时候发布的？我想是去年11月29日。从那天起，我每天醒来都会思考人工智能相关的问题。我尽可能多地阅读相关资料，但还是觉得自己远远落后于这个领域。对我来说，当我跟别人谈论人工智能时，人们通常会分为两类。一类是全身心投入型，真心实意地投入其中。这就像一颗流星朝你飞来。这比移动互联网作为技术变革还要大，甚至可能比互联网本身作为技术变革还要大。它将深刻重塑社会，所以我全力以赴。我已经过了那个阶段，达到了另一个境界。另一类人则持怀疑态度，他们觉得：“我听过太多次炒作了。去年是加密货币，去年是 Web3，这些都失败了。元宇宙也一样。” 所以，我认为很多人对此持怀疑甚至不屑一顾的态度。我不明白为什么。其他技术趋势确实没能成功，但元宇宙正在卷土重来。我努力回想，技术变革总是先有炒作，然后是幻想破灭，接着迎来转机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that little curve.
turns.zh: 是啊，那个小小的曲线。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And I think that's where a lot of people might be, where there was so much hype, it was so noisy, and still is a little bit so noisy that you tune it out a little bit. And, I think, some people have fallen into that camp. I'm all in in the other camp. This is going to radically transform society and it blows my mind even seeing new types of things that come out, like ChatGPT Vision just came out recently, and just seeing the things that people can do with it. And we're just scratching the surface still. So, we're all in, for sure.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得很多人可能处于这种状态，炒作太多，噪音太大，现在还是有点吵闹，以至于你会选择性忽视。有些人就这样陷入了怀疑的阵营。而我则完全投入到另一个阵营。这将彻底改变社会，光是看到 ChatGPT Vision 最近发布，以及人们用它能做出的各种事情，就让我惊叹不已。而我们才刚刚触及皮毛。所以，我们肯定全力以赴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to unpack that. But, I think there's also this camp of people that like, "Yes, something big is happening. I just don't have the time to understand, to build, to play around." What have you found and/or what advice would you share to people that are just like, "I want to go deeper down this rabbit hole. I just don't know where to start, because I have so much work to do already and this isn't a side thing."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想深入探讨一下。但我觉得还有一类人会说：“是的，确实有重大变革，但我没时间去理解、去开发、去尝试。” 你有什么发现，或者能给那些想深入探索但又无从下手的人什么建议？他们会说：“我想更深入地探索这个领域，但不知道从哪里开始，因为我已经有太多工作要做了，这又不是副业。”

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: The advice I have for people, and the advice I have for myself, I'm in that too, I wake up every day to too many emails, and Slack chats, and people knocking on my door, and my desk, and all things. So, this is a challenge for me too. You just have to take the time. There's just no other way for me. And that to me doesn't mean... It's about priorities. It doesn't mean that you need to work crazy hours. I don't believe in working crazy hours. I don't know what hours I work. I don't know, 50 hours a week maybe. I think, beyond that, you start to make bad decisions and things like that. You get tired. And you need to live the rest of your life. You got to put it into your day. Whether that's setting aside dedicated time to read. (00:18:33): Reading is the thing. You got to read. You got to stay up to date, and you got to play with things, and try things. If you don't have ChatGPT... If you don't have a... I can't remember if it's a pro licenser, whatever, but if you haven't upgraded to get access to things like GPT for Vision, where you can take photos and you have the mobile app. And I was going out for dinner last Friday night with my wife. I try not to take work to dinner with my wife. But, I wanted to try it. And, I took some photos of her food. And, you can do all sorts of crazy stuff, like tell you how healthy the meal is or whatever.
turns.zh: 我给别人的建议，也是给自己的建议——我自己也深有体会。每天醒来，我要面对堆积如山的邮件、Slack聊天、敲门声、堆积在办公桌上的待办事项……所以这对我来说也是个挑战。你必须抽出时间。对我来说，没有别的办法。这并不意味着……这关乎优先事项。它并不意味着你必须拼命工作。我不认同这种拼命工作的方式。我不知道自己每周工作多少小时，也许50小时吧。但超过这个时长，你就会开始做出错误的决策之类的。你会疲惫不堪。毕竟你还要过自己的生活。你得把这些时间安排进日常生活。无论是专门留出时间阅读，（00:18:33）：阅读才是关键。你必须阅读。你得跟上时代，尝试新事物。如果你没有ChatGPT……如果没有……我记不清是否是专业版许可证之类的，但如果你没有升级权限，就无法使用GPT for Vision等功能，比如可以处理照片，还有移动应用程序。上周五晚上我和妻子出去吃晚餐。我尽量不把工作带到和妻子共进晚餐的场合。但那天我想试试看。我拍了些她食物的照片。然后你就能做各种疯狂的事情，比如告诉你这顿饭有多健康之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Anyway. You got to try it. You just got to try it. So, my advice people is, you've got to try it. You've got to set aside the time, or it'll pass you by. It does remind me the mobile wave about a decade ago. Again, I was at Google at the time, I was working on the mobile team. So I guess, it was my job to stay on top of things. But, at that time, some companies like Facebook went all in on it, maybe a bit late, but they eventually made the brave decision. I think if people don't explore AI properly, it will leave them behind.
turns.zh: 不管怎样。你得试试看。你就得试试看。所以我给别人的建议是，你必须尝试。你必须抽出时间，否则机会就会溜走。这让我想起大约十年前的移动浪潮。当时我在谷歌，负责移动团队。所以我想，保持敏锐是我的职责。但当时有些公司，比如Facebook，晚了一点才全力投入，但他们最终还是做出了勇敢的决定。我认为，如果人们不正确探索AI，它会让他们落后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me, I think, at Facebook, Zuck, and also Airbnb, Brian did this, is he said, "Any mocks you show me for new product designs have to be in a mobile app or on a mobile web. They can no longer be desktop for now."
turns.zh: 这让我想起，在Facebook，扎克伯格，还有Airbnb，布莱恩也这么做过，他说：“你们给我展示的新产品设计模型必须在移动应用或移动网页上呈现。目前不能再是桌面版了。”

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Right. Yeah. Same with Facebook. Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 对。是的。Facebook也是如此。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess, do you think that that's the way to approach this is as a leader, just, "Everything you bring me needs to have some AI component." That sounds probably not like a good idea, but is there something that you're thinking about, or have done of just convincing people this is where you want to spend your time?
turns.zh: 我猜，作为领导者，你的做法应该是：“你们带给我的任何东西都必须包含AI元素。” 这听起来可能不是个好主意，但你有没有什么想法，或者已经做过什么说服人们这才是你想花时间投入的方向？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, it's harder, for sure. It's harder, because-
turns.zh: 是的，确实更难了。确实更难了，因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You don't want to force it.
turns.zh: 你不想强制推行。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: ... Yeah, a lot of the tech is invisible. We have a machine learning team we've had on here for a long time, so we've been working in this space for quite some time. But, it's funny, even if you go back 18 months, I think if I was on your podcast 18 months ago and you said to me like, "Hey, what do you think about AI?" I would've said something like, "It's not real. Machine learning's real, let's talk about that." So, things change, and my perception of it's changed. But a lot of the improvements are behind the scenes. They're with large language models or different types of things people are building in the background of infrastructure. (00:20:43): So I don't know what it looks like to design mobile mock-ups that are AI mock-ups. But I do think that people need to start really thinking strategically. Maybe it's just not a mock-up stage, but start to think really strategically about their product and whether it's in the line of the media, or it's coming or not. It's not everything is. And if so, for some I think they require a foundational strategic change. Others, it might be less so. But, I think that's actually the head space that I think people need to be in.
turns.zh: 嗯，很多技术都是隐形的。我们有一个机器学习团队，已经在这里工作很久了，所以我们在这一领域已经耕耘了相当长的时间。但说来有趣，就算回溯到18个月前，如果我当时参加你的播客节目，有人问我“你对人工智能有什么看法？”，我可能会回答“这不是真的。机器学习才是真实的，我们来聊聊这个吧。”所以，情况确实在变化，我对它的看法也变了。但很多改进都是在幕后进行的。比如大型语言模型或者基础设施后台的其他技术创新。（00:20:43）：所以我不知道设计人工智能模型的移动原型是什么样子的。但我确实认为人们需要开始真正从战略高度思考问题。也许这不只是原型阶段，而是要从根本上重新审视自己的产品，判断它是否符合媒体行业的发展趋势，或者是否即将迎来变革。并非所有产品都需要如此。但我认为这确实是人们需要具备的思维模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you impact that further? What does that look like to really think deeply about whether your product is in the way of the meteor?
turns.zh: 你能进一步深化这一思考吗？真正深入思考你的产品是否会成为行业变革的阻碍，这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: You can get sidetracked by the technology, for sure. And I do. I just mentioned, hey, going out for dinner and taking a photo of my food. You can get sidetracked by the tech and some of it's really cool. I wouldn't start there. I'd start with the thing your product does. What's the core premise behind it? Why do people use it? What problem does it solve for them? That kind of thing. And then, ask the question. So go back to basics. "Okay, what is my product for? And why do people love it?' And then ask, "Can AI do that?" And for a lot the answer's going to be, "Yes, it can." For some, it might be, "It can partially do it." And then, maybe for others, "It can't do that, at least not yet." (00:22:07): So you're going to need to map what your product does against what AI can do. And AI can do a lot. It can write. I'll give you a list. It can write, it can summarize, it can summarize text, it can write text, it can answer queries, it can find facts, it can scan text, it can scan images. It can listen to your voice and repeat it. It can take actions. That's the next big thing coming. It can take actions, actually do things. It could like, I mean, "Hey AI. Whatever the AI is called. "Change my flight to Tuesday." Right? It can do things like that. (00:22:46): And so, it can do a lot of things. It can build rules. So, I think any product that has any workflow in it, which is almost all B2B SaaS products, any product that has multimedia in it, they're in the media line or whatever. I don't don't know if this metaphor is working. But, the media is coming and they're in its path. And so, for a lot of these products that you just need to look at what AI can do. And then, for some of it'll be replacement. AI would replace, it'll just do it. And, in other places it'll be augmentation. It'll augment. It'll help people as the copilot ideas that are going around. But yeah, I think that you've got to map your product, and what AI can do, and what it will be able to do, and then ask yourself, "Okay, what are we going to do?"
turns.zh: 你肯定会被技术分心，这很正常。我自己也这样。我刚刚提到，出去吃晚餐时拍食物照片。技术确实很酷，但别从这入手。你应该从产品本身出发。产品的核心理念是什么？人们为什么使用它？它解决了什么问题？然后再问自己，AI能做到吗？很多情况下，答案是“能”。有些情况下，答案是“部分能”。还有些情况下，答案是“暂时还做不到”。（00:22:07）：所以你需要将产品功能与AI能力进行匹配。AI能做很多事情。它能写作。我列个清单：写作、总结文本、回答问题、查找事实、扫描文本、扫描图片、听语音并重复输出、执行动作。这是即将到来的下一个重大变革——AI能执行动作。（00:22:46）：所以它能做很多事情。它能构建规则。所以，我认为任何有工作流程的产品（几乎所有B2B SaaS产品），任何包含多媒体元素的产品，都处于媒体行业的轨道上。我不知道这个比喻是否贴切。但媒体行业正在兴起，而这些产品正处于其影响路径上。对于许多这类产品，你只需要看看AI能做什么。有些情况下会被替代，AI直接接管；在其他情况下，则会成为增强工具，就像现在流行的副驾驶概念一样。但没错，你需要将产品与AI的能力进行映射，思考未来可能的发展方向，然后问自己：“好吧，我们该怎么做？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that at Intercom or a different company of, "Here's a problem we're trying to solve? Oh, AI can actually do this fully for us."
turns.zh: 你们有没有在Intercom或其他公司遇到过这样的例子："这里有个我们正试图解决的问题？哦，AI其实能完全替我们处理这个问题。"

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Oh, yeah. I'll give you Intercom first. Again, this date, I think it was November 29th, etched in our head. We have Fergal who was our head of machine learning. And, Fergal just turns around that day and he's like... Okay, I think he tweeted something actually. He had a tweet that day that was like, "This is it. This is the time. This is the moment. This is the before after." I actually often talk about people... because this is a framework I have, before, after moments. This is a before after moment. That was before. And that is after. And everything has changed. So, we literally ripped up our strategy almost entirely, and started again, from first principles and said, "Okay, why do people use Intercom?" Intercom is a customer support product. And then, very soon after that, Sam Altman, who's the founder and head of OpenAI, said, "Hey, one of the first industries that's going to be disrupted is customer service." We're like, "Yep." (00:24:35): So we did. We totally changed how we think, how we work, and we just went heads down and built a product called Fin. We built other things first actually. Fin came later, now that I think about it. But we went all in on it. It was a little bit of a bet the farm mindset. So we've done it. I think other companies like Google and Bard have to do it, and maybe they're a little bit slow, but it's so early in this tech cycle that, I think, they're fine. So yeah, we did. It was hard, but we had to do it.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊。我先讲Intercom吧。这次会议的日期，我记得是11月29日，这一天深深印在我们的脑海里。我们当时的机器学习主管费格尔（Fergal），那天突然转变态度。他在推特上发了一条动态，大意是：“就是现在！就是这个时刻！这是前后对比的分界线！” 我经常跟人说起这种时刻，因为我有一个框架，分成“前”和“后”两个阶段。这就是前后对比的时刻。之前是这样，之后就变了。我们几乎彻底推翻了原有的策略，从头开始，重新思考用户为何使用Intercom。Intercom是一款客户支持产品。很快，OpenAI的创始人山姆·奥尔特曼（Sam Altman）就说：“嘿，首批将被颠覆的行业之一就是客服。” 我们当时就说：“没错！” （00:24:35）：于是我们真的行动了。我们彻底改变了思维方式和工作方式，全力投入开发Fin产品。说实话，我们最初开发的其他产品，Fin是后来才加入的。但我们下定决心一试。这有点像孤注一掷的赌博。所以我们成功了。我认为谷歌和Bard这样的公司也必须这样做，也许他们进展稍慢，但科技周期还早，我觉得他们没问题。总之，我们做到了。这很艰难，但必须要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you share briefly what Finn is just for folks that aren't familiar?
turns.zh: 能简单介绍一下Fin吗？可能有些人不熟悉。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Fin, first and foremost, is an AI chatbot. So, if you think about customer service, people have questions for a business, and historically, that was mostly email, and phone, and mostly ticketing based. You'd file a ticket, a lot of do not reply email, and so on. And then, came along conversational customer support, which is just basic messaging, like WhatsApp or iMessage, like I mentioned earlier. Now, there's bot first experiences and Fin is an AI chatbot, AI first, chatbot first. So the first line of defense for a customer support team is Finn, not a person. And so, it fundamentally changes. The results we've seen with Fin are mind blowing. Our biggest challenge is actually trying to help customer support teams think about organizational change. (00:26:05): The tech is way ahead. It's actually people wrapping their heads around what this means for the role, the teams, loads of cool stuff, like new types of jobs for people, like conversation designers, a job we have where you design the conversations that Fin does or managers. So anyway, that's what Fin is. Fin has expanded. So, Fin is now also in our Intercom inbox. They've placed a people answer queries, customers support queries, and now Fin's in there too, helping the support reps. Suggesting answers for them to use, or helping them rephrase things. So, it's now augmenting people as well as answering questions by itself.
turns.zh: Fin首先是一款AI聊天机器人。从客户支持角度看，用户向企业提问，传统上主要通过邮件、电话和工单系统处理。用户提交工单后，往往得不到回复。这时候，基于对话的客户支持模式应运而生，比如WhatsApp、iMessage等即时通讯工具。现在出现了以聊天机器人为先的体验，Fin就是AI驱动的聊天机器人。所以，客户支持团队的第一道防线是Fin，而不是真人。这从根本上改变了现状。我们使用Fin的效果令人惊叹。目前最大的挑战是帮助客户支持团队思考组织变革。（00:26:05）：技术已经领先太多了。真正难的是让人们理解这对角色、团队意味着什么，还有很多很酷的东西，比如新兴职业，比如对话设计师——我们专门负责设计Fin对话的岗位，还有经理岗位。总之，Fin就是这样的。Fin已经扩展了功能。现在Fin也进入了Intercom收件箱。他们把人工回复的查询、客户支持查询都放进去，Fin也加入其中，帮助客服代表。为他们推荐答案，或者帮助他们重新组织语言。所以现在它既能辅助人工，又能自主回答问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you're one of the few companies that has pivoted fully into AI. And, I think there's a lot of lessons here about how team structures might change, product strategy, priorities, things like that. So I'm curious just to unpack a couple more things here. First of all, what impact have you seen after going all in and going in this direction?
turns.zh: 我认为贵公司是少数完全转向人工智能的企业之一。在此，我想探讨团队架构可能如何变革、产品战略如何调整、优先事项如何排序等诸多方面。因此，我很想深入探讨几个问题。首先，全面投入并朝着这一方向发展后，贵公司见证了哪些成效？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: It's very early, honestly, to be able to answer that properly. And it depends what you measure as success. So, again, there's a lot of hype and buzz with AI. So, if you're measuring it by interest, it's a huge success. Our target customer is customer support. Our customer support manager leader. And so, they're very curious. They're like, "Does it actually work?" Again, back to the earlier thing of there's so much hype, there's a bit of skepticism around it. "Does it actually work? Is it as good as a person?" And in customer support, people who tend to work in that role are typically very high empathy, care a lot about people. And so, they're like, "But is it as good as a person? Is it nice, friendly? Does it understand humanity?" And so, a lot of curiosity, and a lot of interests, and a lot of people trying it. (00:27:57): We have some customers who are hugely successful with it. They can answer up to 50, 60, 70% of their inbound questions with Fin. So we've some customers who see huge success. But it's early. And so, has it transformed our business financially? Not yet. I think, all fast-growing startups... If you think of AI Intercom as, I guess, a new startup, even though we're 900 people, the growth curve, you're looking for this exponential curve, as opposed to big public company linear growth curve. With the exponential one, it takes a while. The first year or two years is the bottom of that. And so, I think we're still in the trying to figure out exactly what's going on, trying to talk to educate people. But, we have enough evidence to believe it's the future for sure.
turns.zh: 说实话，现在要给出准确的答案还为时过早。这取决于你如何衡量成功。人工智能领域当前热度极高，如果以引发的关注度来衡量，那确实取得了巨大成功。我们的目标客户是客服团队，特别是客服经理。他们对此充满好奇，总是追问：“这真的有效吗？”考虑到外界对人工智能的诸多期待，人们对其存在诸多质疑：“它真能替代真人客服吗？能做到和真人一样友善、善解人意吗？”客服人员通常富有同理心，非常关心用户体验，因此他们会反复验证：“它能达到真人客服的水平吗？是否足够友善、亲切？是否理解人类情感？”因此，人们对此充满好奇，兴趣浓厚，许多团队都在尝试应用。（00:27:57）：我们有一些客户使用Fin成功案例，他们能用这款工具处理50%、60%、70%的客户咨询。但这毕竟还处于早期阶段。那么它是否从财务层面重塑了我们的业务？目前尚未显现。我认为所有快速发展的初创公司……如果你把AI Intercom视为新兴初创企业（尽管我们已有900名员工），其增长曲线应是指数级增长，而非大型上市公司的线性增长。指数级增长需要时间，前两年通常处于低谷期。目前，我们仍在探索其核心价值，努力向用户普及相关知识。但我们已掌握足够证据确信，AI必将成为未来的趋势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any examples of either this product or other instances of AI just blowing your mind where you're just like, "Wow, I never imagined it would be this good"?
turns.zh: 是否有任何案例，无论是这款产品还是其他人工智能应用，能让你惊叹不已，感叹“哇，真没想到能如此出色”？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I go back to that before after thing. So, the first version of ChatGPT was a before, after, where we we've been working, like I said, in this space, we've had a machine learning team for a long time. The way our machine learning thing worked before ChatGPT was that there was not a manual setup. A customer support manager would have to orchestrate the bot, and teach it what to say, and just a lot of orchestration, a lot of teaching it. And then, ChatGPT showed up and it's like, "Oh, it can do it by itself." It gets it wrong sometimes. So, do people get the question wrong too? It's as good as a person nearly for a lot of these basic things. So that blew my mind. And then, that was, "Oh, it can answer questions." But then, you're like, it can reason. (00:29:45): There's actually a debate about whether is this reasoning or deduction. But, it can work things out. And, I'm not one for going down into these really philosophical things. I'm like, "We just need to build. Let's go back, build the product." Or whatever. But it can work things out. And that blew my mind. And, we fed ChatGPT and other companies too, we played with other LLMs, like Entropik and so on, it can work things out. And that was mind-blowing. Then you can see it doing things, like writing code. And I was like, "Wow, it's really good at writing code. What does that mean?" And then, you start thinking, here at Intercom we have a one to five ratio. So a PM has about five engineers on a team. And you're looking at this thing writing code and you're like, "What happens next? Do we need as many engineers or will their role change? And they'll start doing different types of things like reviewing code instead of writing code?" (00:30:41): So that blew my mind. And then, the visual stuff, like I mentioned earlier, I think the visual thing was bigger than the original one. It can parse imagery, and it can help you see the world. You take a photo of your bike and say, "Hey, what's wrong?" And It'll tell you what's wrong, how to fix it. You can be traveling, take photos of stuff. It's in a different language. It's etched in stone on a 12th century cathedral. You're like, "What does that say?" And it'll tell you what it says. It's just like how to do that. This is what I'm actually repeating most to people these days, here in Ireland, if you want to be a radiologist, so study X-rays and tell people what's wrong, and so on, and forth, it's seven years training to learn that skill. So, seven years to be a radiologist, and then you're just into the job. AI, it seems it's already better at it. So, it's already better at it, and it can ingest every X-ray ever made. No human can ever read, and think about, and synthesize every X-ray ever made. (00:31:45): So, of course it's better. And then, you're like, "Okay, what happens now?" I guess, the whole job changes. Radiologists will not take x-ray. Well, I guess they might take them. But, they won't analyze them, for sure. They'll look at what AI says, check that it's right, and then it's bedside manner time. Tell the patient, maybe tell them what course. So the job just fundamentally changes. And by the way, that could be amazing. Here in Ireland, we have long queues for hospitals, epic waiting lists for people getting X-rays. So, this is a really good thing possibly for people. Here's the craziest one I have. AI can listen to your voice and copy it, so it can say things and it sounds exactly like you and it's really, really good. Almost in distinguishable. You're like, "That sounds like Paul." And so, I mentioned the Metaverse earlier. I don't know if you saw Zuck talks to Lex [inaudible 00:32:35]. See that?
turns.zh:
让我再回顾一下之前和之后的对比。ChatGPT的第一版可以算是一个转折点。在我们致力于这项技术的这段时间里，我们的机器学习团队已经运作了很久。ChatGPT出现之前，机器学习的工作流程是这样的：没有手动设置流程，客户支持经理需要手动操控机器人，教它该说什么，整个过程充满了繁琐的协调和教学工作。然而ChatGPT的出现彻底改变了这一切——它能自动完成这些任务。当然，它偶尔也会出错，但在很多基础任务上，它的表现几乎和人类一样出色。这真的让我惊叹不已。

接下来是它能回答问题的功能。然后是推理能力（00:29:45）——关于这是推理还是归纳，这里存在争议。但总之它能解决问题。虽然我不太想深究这些哲学问题，但我们只需要专注于产品开发。接着是代码生成功能，我惊叹于它在编程方面的卓越表现。这让我开始思考：在Intercom，我们的PM团队通常配有五名工程师。看着ChatGPT自己写代码，我不禁好奇：未来会怎样？我们是否需要更少的工程师，或者他们的角色会转变？比如从编码转向代码审查？

视觉识别功能同样令人震惊（00:30:41）。它能解析图像，帮助人们理解世界。比如拍张自行车照片问“哪里出问题了？”它能准确指出问题所在。旅行时拍照遇到外文标识？它能翻译成中文。雕刻在12世纪大教堂的碑文？它能准确解读内容。这些功能让我深受启发。如果你想成为放射科医生，现在爱尔兰需要七年培训才能掌握技能。而ChatGPT似乎已经超越了这一门槛。它能处理所有已有的X光片，而人类根本无法完成如此海量的数据处理。

所以，AI显然已经更胜一筹。接下来，放射科医生的工作将彻底变革。他们不再亲自操作X光设备，但会参考AI的诊断结果，进行最终的解释和治疗方案制定。这对患者来说无疑是福音。爱尔兰的医院排队时间漫长，X光预约名单积压严重，AI技术或许能为患者带来革命性的改变。

最令人惊叹的是语音模仿功能。它能模仿你的声音，准确传达你的意思，甚至让人难以分辨真假。还有元宇宙概念，我认为它将彻底改变人类的社交方式。
不知道你有没有看扎克伯格和莱克斯的对话（00:32:35处音频中断）。看到了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: So that was my first, "Oh." For people who haven't seen it, they met in the Metaverse, I think, or some virtual world.
turns.zh: 所以那是我第一次感叹"哦。"对于没看过相关内容的人来说，他们是在元宇宙或者某个虚拟世界里相遇的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was a black room.
turns.zh: 那是一个黑色的房间。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: In a black room. Yeah. And, the tech has come on so they can analyze your face and build a 3D model. It's really good, really, really close. So, you can imagine, that's going to get better. Based on the trajectory of that technology, it's going to get better. And so, the voice thing and the face thing means both of those things are almost indistinguishable from a real person. And, AI will be able to ingest all the things people say and do. And, when people die, it'll be able to replicate that person. And so, there's an afterlife, hey, your parent dies and you can still talk to them. And, that could be the weirdest thing. Maybe it's not good for people. I don't know. But, that tech is just around the corner. And the AI can answer your questions, mind-blowing. It's mind-blowing.
turns.zh: 在一个黑色的房间里。是啊。这项技术已经有了很大的进步，他们可以分析你的面部特征并构建3D模型。效果非常好，真的非常、非常接近真实了。所以你可以想象，未来这项技术会变得更好。基于当前技术的发展趋势，它肯定会不断进步。因此，语音识别和面部识别技术意味着这两项技术几乎可以与真人无异。人工智能将能够记录人们的所有言行。当人们去世后，它将能够复刻那个人的形象。所以会有来世，嘿，你的父母去世后，你仍然可以和他们交谈。这可能是最奇怪的事情了。也许这对人们来说不是好事。我不知道。但这项技术即将问世。人工智能还能回答你的问题，这真是令人惊叹。太令人惊叹了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's actually a Black Mirror episode with that same premise, where-
turns.zh: 实际上《黑镜》有一集也是基于同样的设定，讲的是——

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Yeah. And I don't think it ended well.
turns.zh: ……是啊。我觉得结局不太好。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Be careful.
turns.zh: 小心点。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: For sure. For sure. Yeah, I think, the [inaudible 00:33:48] and the voice translation thing is another one. I can't remember. Maybe it's in Mission Impossible, where it can take a voice, translate it, and translate it in real-time. And this tech is, again, just here, where if I was a native Spanish speaker and couldn't speak English, you and I could still have this podcast. Your voice would be translated in Spanish in real-time for me. It's, again, mind-blowing.
turns.zh: 当然。当然。是啊，我觉得[00:33:48的音频缺失]和语音翻译技术是另一回事。我记不清了。也许在《碟中谍》里，有个场景能实时翻译语音。同样，这项技术已经触手可及。比如，如果我是一个西班牙母语者但不会说英语，你和我仍然可以进行这场播客。你的声音会实时翻译成西班牙语，而你的嘴型也会同步调整。这真的太令人惊叹了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're actually working on dubbing/translating podcast episodes, which is all done through AI, where it figures out what you're saying, makes it Spanish, and then also changes your lips to match. And, we're trying to launch a couple of those. And that's actually very AI-based. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我们实际上正在制作播客的配音/翻译版本，全部通过人工智能完成，它能理解你说的话，将其翻译成西班牙语，然后还能让你的嘴型同步。我们的团队正在努力推出几个这样的版本。这确实非常依赖人工智能。是的。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: That's cool. That's really cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。真的太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that your ENG team might change your thinking, because AI can make them much more efficient and work differently. I'm curious what you've seen actually change on your team, either using AI-ish tools, or just building AI products. What do you think is most different? And I'm curious from the perspective of a team that's trying to think about integrating AI and starting to lean into AI, what have you seen most change and should change?
turns.zh: 你提到你的英文团队可能会改变你的看法，因为人工智能能让他们更高效，工作方式也不同。我很好奇你们团队实际经历了哪些变化，无论是使用人工智能工具，还是开发人工智能产品。你认为最显著的变化是什么？从一个试图整合人工智能并开始依赖人工智能的团队的角度来看，你认为最需要改变和应该改变的是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Ultimately, you need really great machine learning engineers. That's where it starts. And if you don't have that, then you're going to find it hard to build truly, really, truly great things. So, what OpenAI provide, and what Entropik provide, and Claude, they provide an amazing technology, but you got to build on top of it. If you really want something brilliant, you got to build on top of it. So, we adapted what they build for customer support. Maybe someday we need to go build our own LLM that's just for customer support. Maybe. I don't know where that will all go. And maybe everyone will have their own LLM for every single business. I don't really know, to be honest. Maybe these companies will provide specialized LLMs. But anyway, that's the first thing. And, of course, these people are in high demand. So, you need to invest in building out that function, I think. Really invest in building out the function. (00:35:46): So that's what we've been doing. Our ML team's way bigger than it was and way bigger than it ever has been at Intercom. And then, it forks. So, some projects are very heavy on that ML team and it needs them. But other projects are more front end, like the inbox stuff I mentioned earlier, where we have Fin and Fin is working, we've built the underlying technology. Now it's a question of if you have a human support person answering questions in the inbox, that's a natural chat conversational interface, pretty straightforward. What happens when there's now an AI assistant in there? How do they talk? And what do they do? And when do they interject? And how do you represent that in the user experience that feels natural? So that's a really hard design problem. (00:36:32): So, saying back into like, okay, we've a product team that's a product manager, a product designer, maybe three, four, maybe five engineers, and they're getting help from the machine learning team. So, we now have both setups. And increasingly, we can do more with the latter, more teams who can build on the foundational technology that we've been building over the last 12 months or so. So that's one thing. I think a second thing that comes to mind is not to think about it as bolted on. I think some people are still in that camp. (00:37:08): Again, I'll go back to the mobile thing. There's just so many direct parallels with it. Like I said earlier, at Google, I worked in the mobile apps team. I worked on mobile Gmail, mobile docs, and it was the mobile team. And we were in London. We're like, "Hey, we're the mobile team in London." And meanwhile, over in Mountainview in California, no one cared. It's was like, "You're 20 people. We're 200. No one uses this stuff on a phone." And again, a lot of skepticism. "No one's going to write docs on the phone. Seriously? They're going to write a full document on a phone, are you crazy?" So, don't do that. We're trying not to do that. Don't bolt it on. Don't be like, "Oh, we'll have a bunch of AI people..." And we do have some specialists. But generally speaking, we're trying to have everyone learn about it.
turns.zh:
归根结底，你需要真正出色的机器学习工程师。这是关键所在。如果没有这样的团队，你就很难打造出真正、真正、真正出色的产品。所以，OpenAI提供的技术，Entropik提供的技术，Claude提供的技术，它们都是了不起的技术，但你必须在此基础上进行深化。如果你想做出卓越的成果，就必须在现有技术上进行迭代。因此，我们将这些技术应用于客户支持领域。或许未来我们需要为客户支持单独开发专属的LLM模型。谁知道呢，或许每家公司都会为各自的业务打造专属LLM模型。说实话，我对此并不确定。或许这些公司会提供专门的LLM模型。但无论如何，首要任务是——当然，这些人才需求极高。所以，我认为你必须投入重金来构建这一功能，真正下功夫打造这项功能。（00:35:46）：这就是我们一直在做的。我们的机器学习团队规模比以往任何时候都大得多。在Intercom，这是史无前例的。然后，团队会分化。有些项目对机器学习团队的依赖性很强，需要他们的支持；而其他项目则更偏向前端开发，比如我之前提到的收件箱功能。我们有Fin参与开发，底层技术已经搭建完成。现在关键在于，如果让真人客服在收件箱中回复问题，这本质上就是自然的聊天对话界面，相当直接。但当引入AI助手后，会出现什么情况？他们如何交谈？如何执行任务？何时介入？又如何在用户体验中呈现得自然？这是一个非常难的设计难题。（00:36:32）：回到产品团队的架构，比如产品经理、产品设计师，可能还有三到五名工程师，他们会得到机器学习团队的支持。现在我们两套架构并行存在。越来越多的团队能在过去12个月左右开发的底层技术基础上进行创新。这就是关键所在。我认为第二个要点是不要将其视为可随意添加的模块。有些人至今仍持这种观点。
（00:37:08）：再举个例子和移动端的对比，简直如出一辙。正如我之前提到的，我在谷歌时就属于移动应用团队，负责移动版Gmail和移动版文档。当时我们在伦敦，团队自称“伦敦移动团队”。而加州山景城的团队却毫不在意，说：“你们只有20人，我们有200人。没人用手机版的这些功能。”当时大家都充满怀疑，“没人会在手机上写文档？说真的？他们会用手机写完整的文档？疯了吧？”所以别走这条路。我们正努力避免这种模式。不要把它当作可随意添加的模块。别说：“哦，我们会让一群AI专家……” 我们确实有一些专业人才，但总体来说，我们正努力让每个人都了解这项技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, I'm curious just specifically what that looks like, don't bolt it on. The idea there is don't just have a site team that's like, "They're the AI team. They're going to add AI to all this stuff." You're finding and lesson is integrated into every product team.
turns.zh: 有意思。所以我很好奇具体该怎么做，别把它当作可随意添加的模块。关键在于不要让某个团队说：“他们是AI团队，他们会把AI加到所有产品中。”而是将相关知识融入每个产品团队。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: And we're still early there. We're still early. So, what we're trying not to do is have the AI inbox team, and they're the only people who work on AI features in the inbox. I think it's much better to have everyone learn about it. By the way, I'm a big believer in generalists, a big, big believer in... I guess, my background is jack of all trades master of none. That's probably how I describe myself. I've worked as a researcher, designer, PM. And so, I believe in generalists, and so I believe in setting teams up that way. And, yes, specialists matters at times. Machine learning for sure is a deep specialism. And in Intercom, we generally, in engineering too, much prefer people who learn new things, whether it's a new coding language, or framework, or how to design AI interfaces, or whatever, get more people being able to do it.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们在这方面还处于早期阶段。我们仍处于早期阶段。所以，我们努力避免让AI收件箱团队独自开发AI功能。我认为让所有人都能了解这项技术要好得多。顺便说一句，我非常赞同通才主义，非常、非常赞同……我的背景就是样样通、样样松。我就是这么形容自己的。我曾担任过研究员、设计师和产品经理。因此，我坚信通才主义，也支持以这种方式组建团队。当然，专家在某些时候也很重要。机器学习无疑是一项深度专业领域。在Intercom，我们在工程团队中也更倾向于让人们学习新事物，无论是新的编程语言、框架，还是如何设计AI界面等等，让更多人掌握这些技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like, again, your company is a little bit of living in the future, where a lot of companies are going to get to once they realize, "Oh shit. We really need to get big here." Or they're already working on it. I'm curious if there's other maybe pitfalls you ran into that you think people should try to avoid and something you could share there, or just any other lessons about making this transition that you think might be useful to other people.
turns.zh: 我觉得，再说一次，你们的公司有点领先于时代。很多公司一旦意识到“天哪，我们真的需要在这里大展拳脚了”，或者他们已经在为此努力，就会迎来这样的转变。我很好奇，你们是否遇到过其他可能需要避免的陷阱，或者有什么可以分享的经验教训，或者任何关于完成这种转变的建议，对其他人可能有用。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, what I've mentioned so far, don't bolt it on. Stay up-to-date. I mentioned earlier, read, read. I feel like I'm behind all the time. It's moving so fast.
turns.zh: 是的，我到目前为止提到的就是，不要把它当作附加功能。保持与时俱进。我之前提到过，要多阅读、多学习。我感觉自己一直落在后面。变化太快了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are you reading? What do you find is most interesting and informative for reading about what's happening in AI?
turns.zh: 你都在读些什么？你觉得关于AI领域动态，最有趣、最有信息量的阅读材料是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I'd love to tell you that it's incredibly structured. I have a great reading list that I got to read every Sunday morning. It's pretty random. I'm on Twitter, which is now called X, of course, a lot. I follow some people on Twitter. I actually use the recommended feed in Twitter a lot. I think, because I interact and look at a lot of AI, I get to see a lot more. So I do that and I do it deliberately to try and generate more stuff. I'll search Twitter as well. There's loads of cool stuff there. There's some newsletters as well and some people I follow.
turns.zh: 我很想告诉你，它的结构非常清晰。我每周日早上都有一个很棒的阅读清单，内容很随意。我经常使用推特（当然，现在它叫X了），关注一些人。实际上，我经常利用推特的推荐推送功能。我觉得，因为我经常与AI相关内容互动，所以能看到更多相关内容。所以我有意这样做，刻意去获取更多信息。我也会在推特上搜索。有很多很酷的东西。还有一些新闻通讯和我关注的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any newsletters you could call out that you think are most interesting?
turns.zh: 你能推荐一些你认为最有趣的通讯吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, Matt Rickard is one guy who talks a lot about AI. The blogs of companies too. OpenAI have a pretty good blog, and they write papers, and summarize them.
turns.zh: 是的，马特·里卡德（Matt Rickard）是经常谈论AI的人之一。公司的博客也很不错。OpenAI有一个相当不错的博客，他们会写论文并进行总结。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. If there's any other ones you think of, either people on Twitter to follow or newsletters, email me after, and then we'll add them to the show notes.
turns.zh: 太好了。如果你还想到其他值得关注的推特用户或通讯，请之后发邮件给我，我们会把它们添加到节目笔记中。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, perfect. Yeah, yeah, there definitely is. I'll dig them out. Your question earlier, how do you do it? You just try. Try book out half an hour and just go deep for half an hour, and then bookmark a few things, come back to them. Like everyone, you could be so busy, so many distractions, you just got to have to set aside time.
turns.zh: 是的，完美。是的，是的，肯定有。我会把它们找出来。你之前的问题是，你怎么做到的？你就尝试吧。抽出半小时深入研究，然后书签几个内容，回头再看。和大家一样，你可能会很忙，分心事很多，你只需要留出时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other tools or apps that you find really helpful? Sounds like ChatGPT is at the center of how you play around with it. Is there anything else that you find really interesting?
turns.zh: 还有其他你觉得非常有用的工具或应用吗？听起来ChatGPT是你们探索它的核心。还有其他你觉得非常有趣的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I'll try other things like Bard. For example, Bard is Google's AI search engine. Rewind is another fascinating company. I think it's rewind.ai. Rewind is basically augmented AI for your memory. So, install it on your local machine, and it captures everything, and remembers everything. It's all local, so there's no privacy issues. And, you got to try these things to understand whether it's any good, or useful, or where's the boundaries, and how does it work, and so on. So, I'm a believer in that type of thing.
turns.zh: 我会尝试其他产品，比如Bard。例如，Bard是谷歌的AI搜索引擎。Rewind是另一家令人着迷的公司。我觉得它是rewind.ai。Rewind本质上是为你的记忆提供增强型AI功能。只需在本地设备上安装它，它就能捕捉并记录下你的一切生活片段。由于数据全部存储在本地，所以不存在隐私问题。要想了解这些产品是否实用、是否有用、其功能边界在哪里，以及具体运作方式等等，你必须亲自体验一番。所以，我对这类技术深信不疑。
