turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, Intercom is full of diverse opinions about things. And, I think with AI, I'm all in. I'm leaning forward. The media is coming. I'm sold. I'm way past that point. Also, no one knows. No one knows. And so, a lot of the time, when we talk internally, the strong buy-in from Eoghan, our co-founder and CEO, Des co-founder, like me, like a lot of the senior leadership team we're in all in camp. And so, that helps a lot. Of course, if you're senior leadership team in the company are all in, of course, then it trickles down. But equally, some of the hurdles have been like, "Why are you all in?" And I'm like, "An educated guess. A hunch." (00:43:51): The part of business strategy and product strategy that, it's just hard. It's like taste. People talk about product taste, "Who has product taste?" And a lot of it is, it's judgment based on experience. That's all I can say. I don't know. For me, personally, I don't know, I lived through the mobile thing pretty closely, having worked at Google on mobile. I lived through that phase. So, I can see the same type of thing happening now with bigger. So I'm using that experience to go all in. (00:44:23): But it's a challenge for some people, because they don't have that context, or they disagree with it. We have a lot of debate here about the future. Fergal, I mentioned earlier, gave myself and a few other product leaders and Des he gave us a... I don't know, is it a pitch or what? A play? I don't know, about how maybe all of our roadmap with AI is wrong. I don't know if you are familiar with the Horizons framework of Horizon 1, 2, and 3.
turns.zh:
是啊，Intercom里对各种事情的观点五花八门。说到人工智能，我完全支持。我积极拥抱这项技术。媒体浪潮即将到来，我深信不疑。我早已过了怀疑的阶段。不过，坦白说，没人能百分百确定。内部讨论时，我们的联合创始人兼CEO Eoghan、另一位联合创始人Des，还有包括我在内的许多高层管理团队成员，都全力支持。这确实很有帮助。当然，如果公司高层都坚定信念，自然能带动下级员工。但同样的，有些人也会质疑：“为什么你们都这么确定？”我只能说：“这只是个有根据的猜测，凭直觉判断。”（00:43:51）：商业战略和产品战略的部分实在太难了。这就像品味问题。人们谈论产品品味，“谁有产品品味？”很多时候这都是基于经验的判断。我只能说，我个人不确定。我曾在谷歌移动部门工作，亲身经历过移动端的变革。如今我看到类似的巨大机遇。所以我会借助这段经历，全力以赴。
（00:44:23）：但对有些人来说，这挑战太大了，因为他们缺乏背景知识，或者不认同我们的观点。我们内部对未来有很多争论。前面提到的Fergal，给了我和其他几位产品负责人及Des一份……我不知道，是提案还是什么方案？关于我们现有的人工智能路线图可能全错了。不知道你是否熟悉Horizons框架，第一阶段、第二阶段、第三阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Amazon.
turns.zh: 嗯。是的。亚马逊。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. So, Horizon 1 is the medium short to medium term, next 12 months, 12 to 18 months. Horizon 2 being like, "Hey, what's happening?" Whatever, 18 to 36 months out. Or, I think, people use different timeframes, different Horizons. Anyway. We're in Horizon 1 land. We're like, "Yeah, and the next year we're going to do this." And he's like, "Yeah, but two years from now, if this path plays out, everything we're doing now is going to be irrelevant and useless." And you're like, "Oh, okay." And so, those discussions happen. And, the level of ambiguity is off the charts. So, a lot of the challenges have been navigating that ambiguity and helping people get the conviction I have without drying out voices of alternative voices and opinions, which are often valid too.
turns.zh: 对。所以，第一阶段是中短期到中期阶段，未来12个月，12到18个月。第二阶段是，“嘿，情况如何？”不管怎样，18到36个月。或者，我觉得不同的人有不同的时间框架和视角。总之，我们现在处于第一阶段。我们会说：“是的，明年我们要做这个。”他会说：“是的，但两年后，如果这条路径成功，我们现在做的一切都将变得无关紧要和毫无用处。”你会说：“哦，好吧。”所以，这样的讨论时有发生。这种不确定性简直爆棚。所以，许多挑战就在于如何驾驭这种不确定性，让人们获得我所拥有的信念，同时又不压制其他有价值的不同声音和观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does help people get that conviction? Is it just showing them examples of, "Here's something." "Wow, look at this thing. This is unreal." And, I think, partly what helps, I imagine, is the market you're in seems like such a clear opportunity for AI, feels like an easier pitch than maybe a lot of other markets.
turns.zh: 那怎样才能帮助人们获得这种信念呢？就是给他们展示例子，比如：“看这个。”“哇，看看这个，太不可思议了。” 我想，部分帮助在于，我们所处的市场对人工智能来说似乎是一个明显的机会，相比许多其他市场，推广起来要容易得多。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, that's true. For sure. That's true. Yeah, showing people is definitely the easiest way. I think customer support is definitely... Like I said, [inaudible 00:46:20], number one, customer support. So you're like, "Okay, I guess we should adapt." Adapt or die is our mantra. Adapt or die. I think that there are other industries where they're on the same journey, it's just not as obvious. So for example, reporting software, Tableau or any reporting product, how do they work? Well, they're the typical read, write app, build dashboards, filtering, querying, hardcore querying, query database, get some numbers, show it in a UI. A lot of thought and care goes into how you present that data to people. The different types of charts that are appropriate help people make good decisions ultimately. (00:47:04): I think, again, this is hand wave, who knows. Maybe that's all done dead now. And, the reporting product of the future is just a box, and the box just goes to the database, and the box is just, "Who was our best salesman last year January? Okay. Who was our top performing representative in January? Lenny." The report product to the future might look like that. And so, project management tools is another one. There's a bunch of products that I think are just outside the most obvious customer support one. And yet, equally ripe for a newcomer to come with a completely different paradigm and potentially take over.
turns.zh: 是啊，这倒是真的。当然啦。这确实没错。是啊，让别人看看确实是最简单的方法。我觉得客户支持绝对是……就像我之前说的，[00:46:20]，首要任务就是客户支持。所以你会想，“好吧，我想我们应该做出改变。”适应或灭亡是我们的座右铭。适应或灭亡。我觉得其他行业也在经历同样的变革，只是没那么明显。比如，报告软件，比如Tableau或者其他任何报告产品，它们是如何运作的呢？嗯，它们就是典型的读取、写入应用程序，构建仪表板，进行过滤、查询、深度查询、查询数据库，获取一些数据，然后在用户界面中展示。如何把这些数据呈现给用户，这需要花很多心思和精力。适合的图表类型能帮助人们做出正确决策。（00:47:04）：我觉得，再说一次，这只是随便一说，谁知道呢。也许现在这套路已经过时了。未来的报告产品可能就只是一个界面，然后直接连接数据库，界面只会问：“去年1月，我们最好的销售员是谁？好的，1月份表现最出色的销售代表是谁？是Lenny。”未来的报告产品可能会是这样的。还有项目管理工具也是另一个例子。我觉得除了最明显的客户支持领域外，还有很多产品也值得关注。然而，这些领域同样急需新来者用全新的范式颠覆市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that this connects back to your very first point about trying to think about where AI integrates is. Think about what problem are you solving as a company. For example, Tableau, helping people visualize data. And then, the question is, can AI just do this for you? And in that case, oh, and maybe you can. And that gives you basically a whole strategy of like, "Okay, how do we actually do that with AI?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢你把这点和最初关于AI整合的讨论联系起来。想想看，你作为一家公司，到底在解决什么问题。比如Tableau，帮助人们可视化数据。然后问题来了，AI能替你完成这些吗？如果可以，那你基本上就找到了一个全新的策略：好，如何用AI实现这一目标？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And, I don't know if the reporting thing will play out that way. But, if you're a Tableau type company, you've tons of designers who design dashboards, and filters, and querying type workflow. What do they do? The UI is the box. So, it's really hard to get into your head like, "We must..." If you have conviction that we must change really hard.
turns.zh: 是啊。我不知道报告这块是否会朝这个方向发展。但如果你是一家Tableau类型的公司，里面有大量设计师负责设计仪表板、过滤器和查询类的工作流程。他们做什么？界面就是那个框。所以，要想让他们真正领悟“我们必须……”的理念，实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one last question here. For team members learning and starting to work within this realm, is there anything you find helpful to get them ramped up, other than the advice you've already shared, which is just read a lot of stuff, watch Twitter/X, subscribe to these newsletters, and then just try it?
turns.zh: 或许最后再问一个问题。对于刚开始接触这个领域的团队成员，除了你已经分享过的建议——多读相关内容、关注推特/X、订阅新闻通讯然后尝试实践之外，有没有什么其他有用的方法能帮助他们快速上手？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I also try and read things that say it's all a load of crap. So, it's very easy... I've been guilty of this many times. Back to the mistakes you've made. I've been guilty of this many times, where I've jumped on a bandwagon and it was all wrong. And the older I get... The Web3 thing, I'm like, "I don't even know what Web3 is." Crypto, I never bought crypto. Maybe I'm wrong about that. But, I'm not a bandwagon jumper. But, maybe might've been when I was earlier. And I try these days to read the alternative opinion. People who are skeptical or think it's bad. A lot of people think this is terrible for humanity. This technology is going to eat us alive. So, I try and balance my optimism. I'm a delusively optimistic thinker, so I try and balance that with a negativity, I guess.
turns.zh: 我也会尝试阅读那些说这全是胡说八道的文章。所以这很容易……我自己也多次犯过这种错误。回想自己犯过的错误。我也多次跳上某个潮流，结果全错了。随着年龄增长……Web3那事儿，我会说“我甚至都不知道Web3是什么”。加密货币，我从没买过，也许我错了。但我不随大流。不过可能早年我曾这样做过。如今我尽量阅读不同观点。那些持怀疑态度或认为它有害的人的观点。很多人认为这对人类很糟糕。这项技术会把我们吞噬掉。所以，我努力平衡自己的乐观态度。我是个自欺欺人的乐观主义者，所以我会努力用悲观来平衡乐观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really good advice.
turns.zh: 这真是条好建议。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else in this realm that you think might be useful to share before we shift to a different topic?
turns.zh: 在这个领域里，你是否还有其他认为值得分享的观点，以便我们转换到下一个话题？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Oh, yeah. The other thing is, don't be afraid. I think people are a bit afraid of it. And, for example, if I started walking around our office here saying, "Hey, I think we need two engineers per team going forward." That's probably not really a good idea to do that. And I think in reality that's not going to be how it plays out. I just feel like there's loads of great studies over the years about how people don't end up losing jobs, the jobs get moved around. And also, for customer support, for example, it's a high attrition job. So, people saying, "Hey, everyone's going to lose their job. A bot's going to take over." It's like, maybe some of that will happen. But probably to attrition, as in someone quit and just didn't get back-filled. So, the doomsday scenarios that I don't think would play out as much. But, for sure, it's easy to be afraid of it. And, I think you have to lean into it.
turns.zh: 哦，对。还有一点是，别害怕。我觉得人们对此有点恐惧。比如说，如果我现在在我们办公室里四处走动，说：“嘿，我觉得未来每个团队需要配备两名工程师。”这可能不是个好主意。实际上，我认为现实情况不会是这样的。我只是觉得多年来有很多很棒的研究表明，人们并不会因此失业，工作岗位会被重新分配。再比如客户支持岗位，人员流动率很高。所以，人们会说：“嘿，每个人都要失业了。机器人会接管一切。” 但也许有些情况会发生，但很可能是人员离职导致职位空缺，所以那些末日场景不太可能成真。不过，人们确实很容易对此感到恐惧。我觉得你必须勇敢面对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay, I want to chat about frameworks. You have a lot of interesting frameworks you've put out there. So, maybe we do a rapid fire through a number of frameworks that you've worked with and find useful. And, you actually mentioned this before and after, which I hadn't heard about. What's the general idea to that concept?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你这么说的。好吧，我想聊聊框架。你提出了很多有趣的框架。或许我们可以快速浏览一下你用过且觉得有用的框架。还有你之前提到的before和after概念，我之前没听说过。这个概念的大意是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Before, after is literally that simple, I think. We've a rebrand at the moment happening, and that'll be a before, after moment. We're redesigning our pricing. And then, the day that pricing goes live, that would be a before, after, because nothing's the same. And so, we need to go back out and talk to people again. I'm a big believer in talking. You got to talk to customers, it's the only way. You've got to talk, talk, talk, learn, learn, learn. Don't take with the safe face value, go deeper. And so, a lot of these before, after moments, once you've passed, yeah, into the after you got to start learning, "Were we right? Were we wrong? What happened? What do people think?"
turns.zh: before和after其实很简单。我觉得我们目前正在进行品牌重塑，这就是before和after的时刻。我们正在重新设计我们的定价策略。当定价策略上线的那一天，那就是before和after的时刻，因为一切都不一样了。所以，我们需要重新出去和人们沟通。我非常相信沟通。你必须和客户沟通，这是唯一的办法。你得不断沟通、学习、反思。不要只看表面，要深入探究。在很多before和after的时刻，一旦你进入after阶段，你就得开始反思：“我们做得对吗？我们做错了吗？发生了什么？人们怎么想的？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk more about this pricing learning/mistake you shared? What do you think you did wrong? What happened there?
turns.zh: 你能多谈谈你分享的定价学习/错误经历吗？你觉得自己做错了什么？当时发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: We had a principle called align price to value. By the way, I think, pricing is incredibly difficult. A lot of the design team who work in pricing here, I say to them, it's one of the hardest design problems I know. I think onboarding is another one. Onboarding people into a product is also. People are like, "Oh hey, you just design a few steps and it's pretty easy. People will follow the steps." Again, deceptively difficult to design great onboarding. (00:52:30): So, I think pricing is deceptively difficult. But we had a principle around allowing price to value. People should pay based on the amount of value they get in the product, easy to say and incredibly hard to do. Value is subjective. The price, for some person they get 10 units of value. I think that's about $5. Someone else is like, "I'd pay $5,000 for those 10 units of value." So, the biggest mistake was a lot of mistakes compounded. And, this is an area where I think we were risk averse. We've ended up with too many pricing models. We've built on top of old competitive mistakes. And, it took a brave decision to say, "We're going to start again."
turns.zh: 我们的一个原则是"价格应与价值匹配"。说实话，定价这事儿真是难上加难。在这里负责定价的团队成员，我常对他们说：这是我所知最难攻克的设计难题之一。另一个难题是用户引导。引导用户使用产品同样不易。人们总会觉得，"哦，设计几个步骤就行了，用户会照着做的。"但要设计出优质的引导流程，实则暗藏玄机。（00:52:30）所以我觉得定价看似简单，实则暗藏玄机。但我们坚持了"价格应与价值匹配"的原则。用户应该根据产品为其创造的价值来支付费用，说起来容易做起来难。价值是主观的，对某些人而言，价值10个单位，可能只需5美元。而对另一些人来说，为了这10个单位价值，他们愿付5000美元。因此，最大的错误是诸多失误叠加而成。在这方面，我认为我们当时过于谨慎，定价模式过多，还沿用了旧有竞争对手的错误策略。最终，我们需要下定决心重新出发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this feels like it could be a solo episode, just talking through your pricing lessons and journey. Maybe just is there a nugget of wisdom you could share for someone that's trying to think about pricing right now based on your experience?
turns.zh: 哇，这感觉像是一期单人访谈，畅谈你的定价经验和历程。或许你能根据自身经历，为当下正思考定价问题的人分享一些智慧箴言？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Number one thing I would say is keep it simple. Keep it simple. It's so tempting to... With us, for example, a lot of SaaS products have add-ons, where you're like, "Hey, we built X and that's 10 bucks." Or 100,000, depends on what product you're selling. "We built X and that's the price of X. Hey, we've just built Y. Y is awesome and it's a new thing you can do, and it unlocks all these new capabilities. People shouldn't get that for free, because it's a new thing that didn't have. So let's charge more for Y, but that doesn't really work with the other... Okay, let's look at an add-on. Oh yeah, cool. People just add on." But then, later, now you've got people who have the add-on, and people who don't, and then you're like, "Add another thing." And so, we've added tiers, with products, tears, add-ons, tearing in the add-on. Oh my god. People can't understand their bill. So, my advice is keep it simple. Fight so hard to resist the temptation to add extra ways in which you price.
turns.zh: 首先，我想说的是要保持简单。保持简单。人往往很想把事情复杂化。比如我们这儿，很多SaaS产品都有附加功能，你会想："嘿，我们开发了X功能，收费10美元。"或者10万美元，取决于卖的是什么产品。"我们开发了X功能，价格就是X。嘿，我们刚开发了Y功能，Y超棒，是个新功能，能解锁更多新能力。人们不该免费获得这些新功能，因为这是新东西。所以我们要为Y加价，但这和其他功能又不兼容...好吧，再加个附加功能。哦吼，用户直接添加了。" 但后来用户有添加附加功能的，有没添加的，你又说："再加个功能吧。" 于是我们加了层级、产品、附加功能、附加功能的层级。天哪。用户看不懂账单了。所以我的建议是保持简单。拼命抵制添加额外定价方式的诱惑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I didn't think about going into this topic, but I'm glad that we touched on it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我原本没打算深入探讨这个话题，但很高兴我们提到了它。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Think I was talking about scars for life earlier. That's another scar for life.
turns.zh: 想我之前说过，终身难忘的教训。这又是一次终身难忘的教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Let's keep talking about some frameworks. Another that I found that I loved is something that you call differentiation versus table stakes. What's that about?
turns.zh: 好吧。让我们继续聊聊一些框架。我发现还有一个我很喜欢的框架，叫"差异化与底线博弈"。这是关于什么的？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: It's like the Kano model, if you're familiar with that. But, it's very simple. I guess, we took the Kano model and just tried to make this really crazy simple version of it. Again, I'm a little bit allergic to things like this. I even hate myself for bringing up the Kano model. I'm allergic to people over intellectualizing frameworks. And like, "Oh, well if you've seen the new different law..." Of whatever. I'm like, "Keep things simple, practical, and pragmatic. And then, let's all, again, go back to work and start building the product, so that customers can benefit, because that's actually all that matters." And so, difference versus table stakes, very simple. I think people who adopt a product, or buy a product, or switch to a product, there's two driving forces. One is the attraction of the new solution, and that's basically differentiation. So what's different and better? But critically, what's different and better in ways that customers care about? (00:56:00): Again, back to all the failed projects, my lesson for a lot of these was, we were different and better in these Google projects in ways people didn't care about. All sorts of Google projects, like Google Wave was an amazingly innovative product that no one really cared about. So, be different and better in ways people care about. So that's the attraction that's like, "Oh, I want to check out that. That looks cool. I want to check that out. That looks better than what I have today." But, on the other side, there's a entry requirement or table stakes. To play the game, you got to have a certain amount of things. And so, they're table stake features. They're often very boring. They're real basic stuff, boring stuff, and easy to ignore, and easy to not build. (00:56:44): And again, a mistake with Intercom maybe over the years is that we were much more attracted to the differentiation and built a lot of that. So we went through different iterations of our roadmap, sometimes changing over the course of a year or two, where we were all the differentiation to realize that everyone loved it and really wanted to buy, but they couldn't, because we didn't have the basic report that they needed or we didn't have the basic permission feature that they needed. And then, the robot is built based on those... Trading off why do we need more differentiation or trading off why do we need to invest more table stakes? And so, these days, the basic Intercom today is we're 50/50 probably in terms of resources, but it has swung 70/30 in both directions at times. (00:57:26): The last piece about it is, I think it's really powerful to look at a roadmap or look at a proposed roadmap and ask yourself, which of these do things matters more to us, not to us actually to our customers right now? The other thing that we've talked a lot about here internally is if you're a startup and you're entering any established category, customer support for us, big established category, massive, a lot of table stakes, built up over years, decades. ServiceNow, Service Cloud, Salesforce, Zendesk, decades of table stake feature building. So to play the game, you need a lot of the table stakes, unless you have incredible differentiation. So from the early years of Intercom, people just buy us alongside Service Cloud or Zendesk. They just buy us alongside. They're like, "This Intercom thing..." We were like first modern messaging and modern UX. They were like, "We want that for our customers, alongside the big giant bag of table stakes." Because Intercom doesn't have any of those. (00:58:26): Then over the years, we've built the table stakes to a point where, okay, now we can fully play the game and people can switch, so they can swap Zendesk for Intercom. But it took us years to get there. And then hence, if you're a startup, you need to invest a lot more in differentiation. And then, over the years, I think you start to balance the books a bit.
turns.zh:
这就像卡诺模型，如果你对它有所了解的话。但其实很简单。我觉得，我们把卡诺模型简化得极其极端了。我对这类东西有点反感，甚至讨厌自己提起卡诺模型。我特别反感那些把框架过度理论化的人。“哦，如果你看过新的法律……”之类的。我总说：“保持简单、实用、务实。然后大家都回归工作，专注于产品开发，这样用户才能受益，因为这才是最重要的。” 所以，差异化与基本要求之间的区别，非常简单。我认为用户采用或购买产品，或者切换到新产品时，主要有两个驱动因素。一是新解决方案的吸引力，这本质上就是差异化。那么，差异化在哪里？在哪里更出色？但关键的是，差异化必须符合用户关心的痛点。（00:56:00）再说回那些失败的项目，我的教训是，谷歌的许多项目在差异化和基本要求之间平衡不当。谷歌 Wave 就是个极具创新性的产品，但没人真正在乎。所以，要在用户关心的方面做到差异化和出色。用户才会说：“哦，我想试试看。看起来很酷。我想看看。它比我现在用的产品好太多了。” 但另一方面，入门要求或基本要求是必须的。要参与游戏，你得具备某些基础条件。这些就是基本要求。通常很无聊，都是些基础功能，容易被忽视，也容易不去开发。（00:56:44）再说 Intercom 过去可能犯的错误，多年来我们太专注于差异化，开发了很多相关功能。于是我们多次调整路线图，有时一两年内就改来改去，最后发现用户虽然喜欢我们的差异化功能，但因为缺少基本的报告或权限功能而无法购买。然后在机器人开发上权衡——是投入更多差异化，还是优先完善基本要求？如今，Intercom 的基础功能在资源分配上可能各占一半，但有时两者比例会达到 70/30。（00:57:26）最后一点，我认为审视路线图或提案时，问自己“这些功能对我们或客户当下更重要？”非常有用。内部我们常讨论，如果你是一家初创公司，进入任何成熟领域，比如客户支持领域，面对 ServiceNow、Service Cloud、Salesforce、Zendesk 等巨头，他们的表层功能经过数十年积累。Intercom 早期用户只是把我们当作 Service Cloud 或 Zendesk 的替代品。他们会说：“Intercom 不错，但我们需要这些成熟功能。” 因为 Intercom 没有这些功能。（00:58:26）多年来，我们一直在调整。
将桌面赌注积累到一定程度后，现在我们可以全面投入游戏，让用户可以自由切换——从Zendesk转向Intercom。但这花了我们数年时间才做到这一点。因此，如果你是一家初创公司，就需要在差异化方面投入更多资源。随着时间推移，我认为你会逐渐找到平衡之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what's interesting about this is one, it just gives you a way to think about looking at your roadmap. How much are we actually doing? And are we doing too much table stakes? Are we doing too much differentiation? So it gives you a awareness of what's happening. And I think, it's an interesting strategy as a startup like, "Do we spend years doing table stakes and then launch? Or is it go the way Intercom went, like differentiate first we'll build everything else later?" Wonder when it makes sense to go one or the other.
turns.zh: 我觉得这件事的趣味点在于，首先，它能让你以一种全新的视角审视自己的路线图。我们到底在实际做多少事？我们是不是在过度关注基础功能？又或者我们是否在过度追求差异化？这样一来，就能让你清楚地认识到当前的情况。作为一家初创公司，面对这样的策略选择时，你会如何抉择？是花数年时间专注于基础功能后再推出产品？还是像Intercom那样，先专注于差异化，再逐步完善其他模块？什么时候该选择哪种策略才最合理？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And it probably depends on the market, different categories, and all sorts of things. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。这很可能取决于市场环境、不同品类以及诸多其他因素。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Awesome. Okay. The next framework is something that you call swinging the pendulum. What is that about?
turns.zh: 好的。太棒了。接下来要讲的框架叫做“钟摆效应”。这是什么意思呢？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I actually mentioned an example a bit earlier. Differentiation in table stakes was swinging the pendulum. So, swinging the pendulum means, you take a step back from everyday work life, and you make the observation that something's in an undesirable state. So, maybe it's, "Whoa, we've all the differentiation in the world, but people can't adopt the product, because we've never built any of these table stakes. It's undesirable." Or, "Oh, we've now built all these table stakes and we've not been investing in differentiation. And actually, we're not that attractive to people, because switching product is a pain. And we're not just attractive to people. Okay, so this undesirable state." (01:00:08): And then, so you go and fix it, but the temptation is that you over-correct. And we've done this so many times in so many domains, everything from, "Okay, we don't have enough differentiation." A year later, "Oh, wait a minute, we're missing all the table stakes. Okay, we're over there." So, product building is one, people is another one. Building out teams and people. Another big one was, I don't know, maybe five years into Intercom, we were on this high growth trajectory, really good classic startup before our pricing problems. And, we looked around and said, "None of us have done this before. I don't think that's good. Undesirable state. Do we even know what we're doing? We're just a bunch of random people. Do we know what we're doing? We need to hire some experts. We need to hire some experts. If we're going to go up market, we need market people who've done it before." (01:01:07): So, that was undesirable state, fix it by hiring people who've done it before. And then, we hired loads of people who've done it before, and what they did was brought the culture and ways of working of their prior company to Intercom. And so, we totally over-corrected, didn't work out in a lot of cases. In most cases, it didn't work out. Because, we weren't trying to be a bigger company, that already exists. We're trying to be us. So, I think, hiring and building teams is another where we really over-corrected to find out, "Okay, it's a balance here." (01:01:43): Related to hiring, one is generalists and specialists, similar theme. People who've done it before, or people who are specialized. And, we hired a bunch of specialists only to realize that they're not adaptable. And, in Intercom, we have a lot of ambiguity, and we lean into the ambiguity, and people who are highly specialized can thrive in big companies, really thrive. They're invaluable employees. But in a fluid startup-y culture with a lot of ambiguity, they can really drown, really struggle. Maybe the middle of this pendulum, landing in the middle is, "Let's hire someone who has done a bit of it and have a bit of specialism, not much, but enough to try and figure it out." So, we hire a lot of those people today.
turns.zh:
实际上，我之前提过一个例子。表层差异化（table stakes）失控了。所以，表层差异化失控意味着，你从日常工作中退后一步，发现某个事情处于不理想的状态。比如，“哇，我们做了各种差异化，但用户就是不接受产品，因为我们从未构建过这些表层差异化功能。这太糟糕了。” 或者，“我们现在构建了所有表层差异化功能，却没有继续投资差异化。结果发现产品换代太麻烦了，用户根本不买账。” （01:00:08）  
然后，你会去纠正，但往往会矫枉过正。我们在很多领域都遇到过这种情况。比如，“好吧，我们缺乏差异化。” 一年后又发现，“等等，我们缺少了表层差异化功能。” 然后又转向另一端。产品开发是一方面，团队和人员建设是另一方面。再比如，Intercom成立五年左右时，我们正处于高速增长期，堪称典型初创公司，但后来遇到定价难题。回头看，我们意识到：“我们这些人以前都没做过这些。这样下去不行。这是不理想的状态。我们到底在做什么？我们就是一群杂牌军。” （01:01:07）  
于是，我们开始招聘有经验的人，但他们带来的是原公司的文化和工作方式。我们矫枉过正了，结果适得其反。在大多数情况下都失败了。因为我们不是要复制现有的大公司，而是要保持自己的特色。所以，我认为，在团队建设上，我们也容易矫枉过正，最后发现：“平衡才是关键。” （01:01:43）  
在招聘方面，还有通才和专才的选择。招聘有经验的人，还是专才。结果发现，他们适应能力差。在Intercom，我们有很多不确定性，我们拥抱这种不确定性，高度专业化的人才在大公司能大放异彩，但在充满不确定性的初创文化中，他们可能水土不服，举步维艰。或许平衡点在于：“招一些有经验但专业度不算太高的人，让他们去摸索。” 所以，我们现在大量招聘这类人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First of all, I love all these stories of things that don't work out, because a lot of people don't like sharing these. And, this is what people want to hear, like, "Here's not everything was perfect. Here's a lot of mistakes that are made along the way." And, it feels like this framework is a result of just doing this too many times. Is the main lesson here generally avoid swinging the pendulum too far? Because sometimes, it's worth it, like in this case of AI, is like, "No, we're going all in." Or in mobile, it was worth going all in. I guess, yeah, what do you think of when I say that?
turns.zh: 首先，我很喜欢听这些失败案例，因为很多人不愿意分享这些故事。人们想听的是：“并非一切都完美无缺。过程中也犯了很多错误。” 感觉这个框架是经历太多次失败后总结出来的。主要教训是不是要避免把钟摆摆得太远？因为有时候，值得一试，比如AI领域，“不，我们全力投入。” 或者移动领域也值得全力投入。我想知道，你怎么看待这个观点？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: In talking to people about this before, sometimes the conclusion of the conversation is something like, it's the only way to do it. You actually can't do it a different way." And so, maybe the question is really, how high does the pendulum go? Versus, you got to swing it, and then it's like, how far do you swing it? And for sure, you're right. With AI, we are swinging it pretty high. Maybe I overestimated earlier, if AI is in the differentiation camp to mix the frameworks, we're still building a lot of table stakes features too, building depth into the product. And that's 50/50, I think I mentioned 50/50 earlier, so that's 50/50. So, we're not totally swinging it. It's swung, but we're also doing the other thing and balancing things out. So, I think you probably have to swing it. It reminds me to know where the boundary is, is what I was going to say. (01:04:01): It reminds me back to the olden days stories. I remember, at Google, privacy was really top of mind, to the point that it would block decisions, block product progress, just privacy circular conversations, so many circular conversations, and nothing ever got built or shipped. I worked on a project for a year at Google and we shipped nothing in the year, just circular conversations, which killed me at the time. So, when I went to Facebook, I realized they have a different approach to privacy. And again, I'm not advocating it's necessarily good, it certainly didn't help their brand. But, there was an idea that to know where the boundary is, you got to across it. And crossing it is painful. But, if you don't cross it, you'll never know. So if you think you're going up to the boundary and you stop before it, turns out it's actually miles over there. (01:04:54): So I think with a lot of this stuff, you don't really have a choice. You got to cross the boundary, feel the pain, be humble enough to realize you didn't get it right, and go again or whatever the corrective course is.
turns.zh:
之前和人们谈论这个话题时，对话的结论往往是：“这是唯一的解决办法。你根本无法用其他方式去做。” 所以，也许问题在于，钟摆能荡多高？相反，你必须先把它摆动起来，然后再问：你能把它荡多远？当然，你说得对。在人工智能领域，我们确实把钟摆荡得很高了。如果说人工智能处于差异化阶段，整合各种框架，那我们仍在开发许多基础功能，为产品注入深度。这两者各占一半，我之前提到过是50/50的平衡。所以，我们并没有完全把钟摆荡到极限。它确实在摆动，但我们也在做其他事情，保持平衡。所以，我认为你可能必须把钟摆荡起来。这让我想起要知道界限在哪里，这就是我想说的。  
（01:04:01）：这让我回想起过去的经历。我记得在谷歌时，隐私问题被视为头等大事，以至于阻碍了决策，拖慢了产品进展，人们只是在循环讨论隐私问题，最终什么也没建起来或上线。我在谷歌做了一个项目，一整年都没上线，就一直在循环讨论，这让我当时很抓狂。所以，当我去Facebook时，我意识到他们对隐私有不同的处理方式。我不是说他们的做法一定好，但这确实没能提升他们的品牌形象。但他们的理念是，要知道界限在哪，就必须跨越它。跨越界限很痛苦，但如果你不跨越，就永远无法知晓。所以如果你以为自己快到界限了，却在界限前停下，那结果可能离界限还有很远。  
（01:04:54）：所以我觉得在很多事情上，你其实别无选择。你必须跨越界限，承受痛苦，谦逊地承认自己做得不对，然后重新开始，或采取其他纠正措施。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, get that pendulum off the even pivot thing that it's on. And then, let's fix that pendulum. Let's put it back.
turns.zh: 是啊，把钟摆从它所在的平衡点上移开。然后，让我们修理那个钟摆。把它放回去。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another framework that I read about briefly, and I love the general idea of it already, which is something that I think you call product market story fit.
turns.zh: 好的。还有一个框架，我简单了解过，我已经很喜欢它的总体思路了，我觉得你称之为产品市场故事契合度。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that?
turns.zh: 那是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: So yeah, with product market fit, pretty basic, well understood, very important. The way I describe product market fit is, you've got to build the right product for the right market. I think, by the way, as an aside, not enough people think about the market side of that equation. A lot of product people don't think about the market side. But for me, it's very simple. The market is the people, the problems they have, and how important the problems are to them. To have a good market, you need a lot of people with the same problem, and they need to care a lot about it. Going back to the Google social stuff, we found a lot of people with the same problem, but they didn't really care. They didn't really care. What they had was fine. So a lot of people with the same problem and a lot of energy around the problem and the product is the solution to that. The market's the who, the product's the what. (01:06:21): And, I don't know, in my career again, so a bunch of products that were built, there were good products in good markets, and they failed and I couldn't work it out. And eventually, I came back to this idea that... And maybe someone might say, "Paul, it's marketing. You're talking about marketing." But story, the story's wrong or the story's missing. And so, sometimes, it would be a great product in a great market explained in a convoluted way. I see that a lot. I used to see that a lot at Google again, just explained in a very complicated way over intellectualized. And, as a result, people are like, "What? What are you talking about?" You don't get their attention. And so, the story is really important, as important. And actually, sometimes you'll see not great products, certainly worse on paper... I'm trying to remember the Spotify competitor back in the day, people were like... What was the name of it?
turns.zh: 是的，关于产品市场契合度，这是一个相当基础且易于理解的重要概念。我对产品市场契合度的理解是，你必须为正确的市场打造正确的产品。顺便说一句，我发现很多人没有充分考虑市场层面的问题。很多产品经理都忽略了市场层面。但对我来说，这很简单。市场就是用户群体、他们面临的问题，以及这些问题对他们的重要性。要想拥有一个好的市场，就需要有大量面临相同问题的人，并且他们必须对这些问题高度重视。回到谷歌社交项目，我们发现有很多用户有相同的需求，但他们并不在意这个问题。他们觉得现有产品已经足够了。所以，相同需求的大量用户群体，再加上对产品的高度关注，这才是解决方案。市场就是用户群体，产品就是产品本身。（01:06:21） 还有，我不知道，在我的职业生涯中，很多产品都失败了，明明是好产品，市场也不错，但还是失败了。我至今也想不明白原因。最终，我回归到这个观点……也许有人会说：“保罗，这就是市场营销啊。你在讲营销啊。”但故事讲得不对，或者故事本身有缺失。有时候，一个优秀的产品在优秀的市场上，但解释得太复杂。比如，我在谷歌就经常遇到这种情况，人们会觉得：“什么？你在说什么？” 根本吸引不了注意力。所以，故事的讲述真的很重要，同样重要。有时你会看到一些不算出色的产品，纸面上的表现更差……我努力回想一下当年Spotify的竞争对手叫什么来着？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ordio?
turns.zh: Ordio？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, Ordio. Ordio was one of these where-
turns.zh: 对，Ordio。Ordio就是那种——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like Ordio a lot.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢Ordio。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: ... Yeah, all I've ever heard about Ordio was, "Amazing product."
turns.zh: ……是啊，我听过的关于Ordio的评价都是“很棒的产品”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: It's failed. And why did it fail? Spotify and Ordio had the same market. They were solving the same set of problems. Ordio was arguably the better product at the time. I don't know if that's true, but arguably the better. I also think Spotify's an incredible product. But, they got the story wrong. And so, again, I think, all product people, whether you're a designer, product manager, people in research, data science, need to think about the story all the time. Work of marketing, work of product marketing, and learn about how to explain the product, as much as how to build the product.
turns.zh: 但它还是失败了。为什么失败了？Spotify和Ordio面对的是同一个市场，解决的是同一组问题。Ordio当时可以说是个更好的产品。我不知道这是不是真的，但至少可以说更出色。我也认为Spotify是个了不起的产品。但他们把故事讲砸了。所以，我认为所有产品从业者，无论是设计师、产品经理、研究人员还是数据科学家，都需要时刻思考这个故事。产品营销的工作，也是产品营销的工作，要学会如何解释产品，以及如何打造产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Makes me think about positioning and how important that is. And, we had April Dunford on the podcast very recently talking a lot about that.
turns.zh: 嗯。这让我想到定位，以及它有多重要。我们最近在播客上请了April Dunford，她对此讲了很多。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, she's excellent. Yeah, it is really, "Why are you better and can you explain why you're better?"
turns.zh: 是的。是的，她很棒。没错，关键在于“你为什么更好，能否解释清楚为什么你更好？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an important point. A final area I wanted to touch on is jobs to be done. So we had the co-creator of Jobs to be Done on the podcast. We had Shyam Krishnan on the podcast. They very much disagree about how effective Jobs to be Done is. I know you guys are big on Jobs to be Done. So, what are your just general thoughts on the Jobs to be Done framework? How effective was it for you all? How do you use it? What do you find work? Doesn't work? Whatever comes up.
turns.zh: 这一点太重要了。最后我想谈谈"待办工作"（Jobs to be Done）这个框架。我们在播客中邀请了"待办工作"框架的共同创始人夏姆·克里希南（Shyam Krishnan），但他们对"待办工作"框架的有效性存在很大分歧。我知道你们都非常推崇这个框架。那么，你们对"待办工作"框架的总体看法如何？它对你们有多有效？你们是如何应用它的？有哪些方面效果显著？哪些方面效果不佳？欢迎畅谈想法。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. I'll be totally honest, at the risk of finding people do this, we worked with Bob West years ago. I think Bob's a great guy. And we followed that model of Jobs to be Done more than the ODI, I think, is the other skill of thought. Anyway. I'll try say this in a simple way. We found Jobs to be Done really good. Very, very useful. But, in a very simple way... Again, back to this idea of simple frameworks, in a simple way, separately, there's so many people who spend so much of their energy debating the nuances and peculiarities of one version. Who cares? No one cares. Oh well, I don't care. They care obviously. But your customers don't care. People you're trying to build a product for don't care,. No one cares. That's a cool intellectual debate. But, for me, maybe this is too extreme. It doesn't really have any place in the work we do. We're just trying to build a great product. (01:09:50): And so, for us with Jobs to be Done, it was a really good way of us centering on the customer problem, focusing on not getting distracted, basing it in good solid research informed insight, that told us the thing people are trying to do. What is the thing people are trying to do? Again, energy. Do they have a lot of energy around it? Maybe the energy thing might've come from talking to Bob actually, now that I think about it. I think it did actually. I think, the idea of this idea that you need people who have a lot of energy around the problem. And you have to interview them for that most of the time to feel the energy they have. It's very easy to see if someone's apathetic versus into it. (01:10:30): So, we've had it pretty good. And, we invented this job stories thing by accident. I can't remember exactly what happened. But, I wrote out this way of writing a job story basically. Well, we didn't call it job stories, someone else called it that. We just, at the time, were like... I can't even remember. It was a trigger. And, anyway, we didn't even give it the thing a name, someone else named it, I think. And, I'm just like, "We're just trying to build a great product." So, we've had it really good in that way, really simple. And then, the other one that we use a lot still here is the four forces, which is this framework of Jobs to be Done. The four forces being... There's different forces when people try and switch product. And some of it's the differentiation, table stake stuff, like the attraction of the new solution, the reasons that you might not adopt it. Habits. People have anxieties. (01:11:26): Here's another funny story to tell you how much... The four forces is really good. Here's a funny story, I was saying earlier that Eoghan and Des were trying to convince me to leave Facebook, which I loved at the time, join and to come. They wrote out the four forces for me to join. And then, secretly, over a few beers, talked to me and fed me my anxieties. And basically worked me on the four forces. And I was like, "That is genius. That is ingenious. Maybe it's a bit... But it's ingenious." And so, the four forces is incredibly good at helping understand why people make decisions.
turns.zh: 是啊。我得坦白说，虽然可能会有人这么做，但我们多年前确实和鲍勃·韦斯特合作过。我觉得鲍勃是个很棒的人。当时我们更关注"工作完成理论"（Jobs to be Done），而非其他分析框架（ODI），我认为这才是另一种思维方式。总之，我尽量用简单的话来说。我们发现"工作完成理论"确实很棒，非常实用。但用最简单的话说……再说回简单框架的概念，以单纯、独立的方式来看，太多人把精力耗费在讨论某个版本的细微差别和特殊性上。但谁在乎呢？没人在乎。哦，我不在乎。他们显然在乎。但你的客户不在乎。为你打造产品的那些人不在乎。没人在乎。这是场不错的学术辩论。但对我而言，或许这太极端了。它在我们工作中没什么立足之地。我们只想打造一款出色的产品。（01:09:50）对我们来说，"工作完成理论"是以客户问题为核心、避免分心的好方法。它基于扎实的研究和洞察，告诉我们人们试图达成的目标。人们试图达成的目标是什么？再说回精力问题。他们对此是否充满热情？也许这种热情源自和鲍勃的交谈，现在回想起来确实如此。我认为确实如此。这种理念强调需要对问题充满热情的人，而这往往需要通过访谈来感受他们的热情。能轻易分辨出他们是冷漠还是充满热情。（01:10:30）我们用得很顺手。后来我们偶然发明了"工作故事"这个方法。我记不清具体过程了。但我写下了基本的写作框架。嗯，我们当时没叫它"工作故事"，是别人后来这么叫的。当时我们只是……我都记不清了。这只是个触发点。反正我们甚至没给它起名，应该是别人起的。而我只想说，"我们只想打造一款出色的产品。"所以在这方面我们用得很顺手。另一个我们至今仍常用的框架是四大力量模型，这是"工作完成理论"的延伸。四大力量模型适用于人们试图更换产品时的不同情境。有些是差异化因素，有些是核心诉求，比如新解决方案的吸引力，还有可能阻碍你采用它的原因。习惯。人们有各种担忧。（01:11:26）再讲个趣事。四大力量模型真是太棒了。我之前说过，埃奥汉和德斯试图说服我离开Facebook（当时我还很喜欢Facebook），加入他们。他们为我写下了四大力量模型，解释加入的理由。然后他们偷偷地，在喝了几杯啤酒后，和我聊天，剖析我的顾虑。基本上就是用四大力量模型说服我。我当时就想，"这太天才了。这真是天才之作。或许有点……但确实天才。" 所以四大力量模型在理解人们决策背后的原因方面真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that a lot of your advice just continues to come back to, keep it simple, cut away anything that isn't necessary. And, I find the same exact thing with Jobs to be Done. I find it really useful as a framework for the podcast, the newsletter, but I think there's this endless set of processes and ways of optimizing that gets people distracted. And, often just slows everything down.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你提出的许多建议，总能归结为一句话：保持简单，剔除不必要的东西。同样，我在“待办事项完成理论”（Jobs to be Done）中也发现了这一点。这个框架对我的播客和时事通讯非常有用，但我发现人们总会陷入无穷无尽的优化流程和方法中，结果反而分心了。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And it's interesting and fun to talk about sometimes, really fascinating, unless you're an academic. But if you're working in a company that you're trying to build a software product for people to improve their lives in some small meaningful way, it doesn't matter. Just use the thing that helps you do that. That's the goal. And use the thing that helps you do that. And that's it.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。有时候谈论这些话题挺有趣的，也很引人入胜，除非你是个学者。但如果你在一家公司工作，致力于为人们开发能切实改善生活的软件产品，关键就只有一个目标：用最有效的工具达成目标。就用能帮你实现目标的工具，仅此而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，现在我们要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I'm ready, yeah.
turns.zh: 我准备好了，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, the two books I recommend to everyone always, I have copies in my office here, It's Not How Good You Are, It's How Good You Want to Be. It's a book by Paul Arden who worked in advertising a long time ago. It's an excellent book. It shows people that you feel an unlimited potential if you think about it the right way, everyone does. The second book I recommend to everyone and buy for people and give to them is Principles by Ray Dalio. I'm a big fan of Ray Dalio. I think he's incredible. I'm a big believer in principles. A lot of us at Intercom are... I always get those two books. And they're totally different. The Paul Arden book, you can read it in 20 minutes. Principles is that thick.
turns.zh: 是啊，我总是向所有人推荐的两本书，我办公室里就放着副本。《不靠天赋，靠决心》（It's Not How Good You Are, It's How Good You Want to Be）。这本书的作者保罗·阿登（Paul Arden）曾在广告行业工作多年，是一本很棒的书。它向人们展示，只要用正确的方式思考，就能挖掘出无限的潜能，每个人都是如此。第二本我向所有人推荐的书，也是我会为别人购买并赠送的书，是雷·达利奥（Ray Dalio）的《原则》（Principles）。我是雷·达利奥的忠实粉丝，觉得他非常了不起。我深信原则的重要性。我们公司很多人都深信这一点……我总是会推荐这两本书。它们截然不同。保罗·阿登的书你20分钟就能读完，而《原则》却厚得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Most recent is The Bear, which I came to late. The reason I love the show is because I think it somewhat celebrates the grind. And I think that's important. I worked in coffee shops a lot when I was younger, when I put myself through college and stuff. And, the grind is part of life, and the grind is a necessity to get things done, and make great things happen sometimes. And I like that about it. I really like that about it.
turns.zh: 最近看的《熊镇》（The Bear）让我相见恨晚。我喜欢这部剧的原因是，它在某种程度上赞颂了奋斗精神。我觉得这很重要。我年轻时在咖啡店工作过，用这份收入支付大学学费。奋斗是生活的一部分，也是完成任务、创造伟大事业的必要条件。我很欣赏这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite interview question you'd like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 你最想问求职者的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, I'll give you a slightly different answer. I don't really have certain few questions for candidates. And I don't like answer question diversity. I don't like questions that rely on memory. Like, "Tell me about the last time you did X." Here's an amazing question I got given recently by Alyssa who used to work here. I had to do referral calls. So, you're interviewing someone, you want to give them the job and they've got referees, and of course, the referees they have are the best people that they've ever worked with and their favorite managers. So this question is, "What feedback will I be giving this person in their first performance review?" It's an amazing question, because the person can't dodge it. There's an answer. And, it's incredibly enlightening.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会给出一个稍微不同的答案。我没有固定的几个问题要问求职者。我也不喜欢多样化的面试问题，不喜欢那些考验记忆力的题目，比如“说说你上次做X的事”。最近Alyssa给我提了一个很棒的问题。她以前在我们公司工作。你要面试某个人，想录用他们，他们有推荐人，而推荐人往往是他们共事过的最优秀的同事和最喜欢的经理。所以这个问题是：“在他们的第一次绩效评估中，我会给出怎样的反馈？” 这个问题很棒，因为求职者无法回避。答案很明确，而且非常有启发性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's a question you ask on reference calls?
turns.zh: 这就是你在推荐电话中会问的问题吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, on reference calls.
turns.zh: 是啊，关于背景调查电话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good question. I love it.
turns.zh: 这真是个好问题。我太喜欢了。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, it's a amazing question. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，这个问题太棒了。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, what a gem. Thank you for sharing that. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 好吧，你真是个宝藏。谢谢你分享这个。你最近发现的自己特别喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: This is maybe cheating, but I go back to a lot of the AI products. I think ChatGPT Vision is mind-blowing. I've been playing with Rewind lately. I was a bit late to it. Des, and Kiran, and a bunch of people here, founders of Intercom, love Rewind, use it and love it. Thing's amazing. So I'm a bit late to that. But, it's just augmented memory. It's mind-blowing. So, Rewind's been fun.
turns.zh: 这可能有点不算新奇，但我最近一直在用很多AI产品。我觉得ChatGPT Vision简直令人惊叹。我最近一直在玩Rewind，不过我入手得有点晚。Des、Kiran还有这里很多人，比如Intercom的创始人，都超爱Rewind，用了之后赞不绝口。这东西太棒了。虽然我入手得晚，但它就是增强记忆功能，简直太神了。所以用Rewind真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they just came out with a little audio thing that can record your actual day.
turns.zh: 他们刚推出了一个能记录你真实日常的音频功能。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, I'm not so sure about that.
turns.zh: 是啊，我对这个不太确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, got some flack.
turns.zh: 是啊，还被不少人吐槽过。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm not so sure. I don't know. I don't know if it's real. It looked like not a real product when they launched in, but I think it's real.
turns.zh: 我不太确定。我不知道。我不确定这是不是真的。他们刚推出的时候看起来不像真品，但我觉得应该是真的。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: And it tippy-toes into what's okay and not okay with AI. And, yeah. Yeah, it's a cool theory though, for sure.
turns.zh: 这也涉及到人工智能中哪些行为是可以接受的，哪些不可以。嗯。嗯，不过这确实是个很酷的理论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite life motto that you often come back to share with people, find helpful for yourself?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个最喜欢的座右铭，经常拿来和别人分享，对自己也很有帮助？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, I have a post-it on my monitor that says, "Only work on what matters most." It's on my monitor, a post-it. And it sometimes falls off, and I have to write it again. Only work on what matters most. And, it's amazing. I go into work, someone emails me, and I'm like, "Oh, God." I'm like, "Only work on what matters most." The second one related is, stop worrying about things you can't control. And so, I have two of those. And so, only working what matters most. Stop worrying about things you can't control. It just reduces the temperature. Again, life lessons learned. I sent a lot of dumb emails in my past, like, "Red Energy, oh my God, what are they thinking?" You wake up in Dublin to a San Francisco email. And you're like, "Oh god. Keyboard." And, if your monitor says these two things, you just don't do that. You just take a breath, get a coffee, come back. Does it really matter?
turns.zh: 是的，我在显示器上贴了一张便利贴，上面写着：“只专注于最重要的事。”它贴在我的显示器上，便利贴有时候会掉下来，我就得重新写上去。只专注于最重要的事。还有一个相关的建议，就是别担心你无法控制的事情。所以我有两个这样的座右铭。一个是只专注于最重要的事。另一个是别担心你无法控制的事情。这真的能让人冷静下来。再次说，这些都是人生经验。我过去发过很多愚蠢的邮件，比如，“红能量，天哪，他们在想什么？”你早上在都柏林醒来，收到旧金山发来的邮件。你会想，“天哪，键盘。”如果你显示器上写着这两句话，你就不会那么做了。你只需要深呼吸，喝杯咖啡，回头再看。这真的重要吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. The second one, I think, I learned first from Seven Habits of Highly Effective People. Have you read that?
turns.zh: 太好了。第二个，我最初是从《高效能人士的七个习惯》中学到的。你读过那本书吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just think about the focus, the circle of things you can control, and then there's the circle of things you can influence, and then there's the things you have no control over. And, I find that really helpful myself. I love that you have it as a post-its. I feel like, I need to make post-its of all these lessons people share as their little mottos.
turns.zh: 只要想想焦点，能控制的事情的范围，然后是能影响的事情的范围，再然后是无法控制的事情的范围。我自己觉得这很有帮助。我喜欢你把它写在便利贴上。我觉得，我需要把人们分享的这些小座右铭都做成便利贴。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, the post-it on the monitor is a real life hack, I found a few years ago. Because it's dumb in a way. The posts on the monitor, it's in the way.
turns.zh: 是的，显示器上的便利贴是我几年前发现的一个实用方法。因为它在某种程度上很蠢。显示器上的帖子总是挡着路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, you actually put it on the monitor in the way of your screen?
turns.zh: 等等，你真的把它贴在显示器上，挡住了屏幕？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: It's in the bottom left, just covering the bottom. Because otherwise, if it wasn't there, I wouldn't look at. I make myself look at it.
turns.zh: 它在左下角，正好挡住了底部。要不然，如果它不在那儿，我根本不会去看。我故意逼自己去看它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Wow. I haven't heard of people putting it over precious real estate on their monitor.
turns.zh: 是啊哇。我还从没听说过有人把它贴在显示器的黄金位置上。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That works. What's the most valuable lesson your mom or your dad taught you?
turns.zh: 这样挺管用的。你父母教给你的最宝贵的人生经验是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: The biggest one, again, so reductive and simple is to be nice to people. I think, being nice goes way further than people really realize. One thing that I've learned, again, the hard way through life is you have no idea what's going on in people's lives. You've no idea. People could have all sorts of really stressful, all sorts of personal stuff going on, and the reason they did the thing at work that you didn't like is because of that. And so, I try and think, "Be nice. You don't know what's going on. You might learn later. Don't act in a way you would regret." I think, being nice in life goes far further than most people give a credit for, because it's too much of a, I don't know, fluffy truism or whatever.
turns.zh: 最重要的一条，也是最简单易懂的一条，就是对人友善。我觉得，友善的力量远超人们想象。我从生活中得到的深刻教训是，你永远不知道别人在经历什么。你真的不知道。别人可能正承受着各种压力、各种个人困境，而他们在工作中做出让你不满的行为，可能就是因为这些因素。所以，我会提醒自己：“保持友善。你永远不知道别人在经历什么。说不定日后你会明白的。别做出让自己后悔的事。” 我认为，在生活中，友善的力量远比大多数人想象的要强大得多，只不过这听起来太像是空洞的陈词滥调了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I 1000% resonate with that. I've been told I'm too nice and I had to become a little less nice. But, I still can't lose that. So I fully buy into that. My parents taught me a similar lesson.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同这一点。我曾被说太善良了，不得不变得不那么友善。但我还是无法失去这种品质。所以我完全认同这一点。我的父母也教会了我类似的道理。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah. And sometimes it's hard. I'd never fired anyone before I joined Intercom, for example. I really did not like doing it. And, since then, I've done it quite a few times in a bunch of different circumstances, and realized it always works out for both sides. And the nicest thing to do is to do the harder thing. It's actually the nicer thing to do. People are relieved in this example. It's a nicer thing to do. So, it can be a complicated one.
turns.zh: 是啊。有时候这很难。加入Intercom之前，我从未解雇过任何人。当时我真的不喜欢这么做。但从那以后，我在各种情况下多次这样做过，结果发现这对双方都有好处。做更难的事才是最善良的选择。实际上，这才是最善良的做法。在这个例子中，人们会松一口气。这才是善良的做法。所以这确实是个复杂的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Final question. You're Irish, you're based in Ireland. What is an Irish food you think people should definitely try out if they ever visit Ireland?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。最后一个问题。你来自爱尔兰，现在在爱尔兰工作。如果有人去爱尔兰旅游，你认为他们一定要尝试的爱尔兰美食是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Can I cheat and say Guinness? Is that food?
turns.zh: 我能偷个懒说健力士啤酒吗？那算食物吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: The Guinness in Ireland. People talk about this and it's true. The Guinness in Ireland is much, much better for a whole bunch of reasons. It's basically a fresh product and it's brewed here. It's the way they think about, it's like milk. Milk goes off, Guinness goes off. Guinness is older than a few days old, tends to start deteriorating. So, Guinness Ireland is amazing, because it's made here. The other thing I think that Ireland does really well is fish. Ireland has not had, by the way, the greatest reputation for culinary excellence over the years. I think Irish food in the States in particular is not good. But, the fish here is incredible. You can get incredible fish. And Ireland's obviously an island, so there's a lot of fish.
turns.zh: 爱尔兰的健力士啤酒。人们都说这话，是真的。爱尔兰的健力士啤酒要好得多，这有诸多原因。它基本上是新鲜产品，在本地酿造。这里的人把它视如珍宝，就像牛奶一样。牛奶会变质，健力士啤酒也会过期。爱尔兰的健力士啤酒更胜一筹，因为是在本地生产的。另外，我认为爱尔兰在鱼类方面做得很棒。顺便说一句，爱尔兰多年来在烹饪方面的声誉并非最佳。我觉得美国的爱尔兰菜尤其不怎么样。但这里的鱼真是令人惊叹。你能买到超棒的鱼。爱尔兰毕竟是个岛国，所以鱼类资源丰富。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the Guinness front, is there any way to get the good stuff not in Ireland? Or is that just you got to go?
turns.zh: 关于健力士啤酒，有没有办法在爱尔兰以外买到优质产品？还是说非得亲自去爱尔兰？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: No, there is actually. You just need to be near a brewery. So Guinness is brewed in Nigeria. There's a huge Guinness market in Nigeria.
turns.zh: 不，实际上有办法。你只需要靠近啤酒厂就行。健力士啤酒在尼日利亚也有生产，尼日利亚的健力士市场规模巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did not know that.
turns.zh: 我之前都不知道这回事。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I think they actually use a different recipe, but it's brewed there. I think the brewery in the U.S. is somewhere in the east coast between New York and Eastern Canada. So, it's somewhere there. So, often, the Guinness in New York can be actually pretty good. The Guinness in San Francisco tends to be really bad. I remember talking to someone about this that works in Guinness. One of my friends, does a lot of work in Guinness. I think the boat carried the Guinness goes down through the Panama Canal back up to San Francisco. So, it's 12-weeks-old or something.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们用的配方其实不同，但啤酒是在当地酿造的。美国的啤酒厂应该在东海岸，纽约和加拿大东部之间。所以就在那片区域。通常纽约的健力士啤酒还是挺不错的，但旧金山的就比较难喝了。我记得和健力士的一位员工聊过这个。我有个朋友在健力士工作很久了。据说健力士的啤酒是通过船运的，先经巴拿马运河，再运回旧金山。可能有12周的运输时间吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Did not think we would be learning about the travel path of Guinness from-
turns.zh: 哇哦。真没想到我们会从——

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: At least this is what I've heard. The Guinness has so many myths, you just don't really know what's true. But, these are the stories I've been told.
turns.zh: 至少这是我听说的。健力士有很多传说故事，真假难辨。不过这些都是别人告诉我的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Amazing. Paul, you are awesome. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: ……太神奇了。保罗，你太棒了。非常感谢你能来参加节目。最后两个问题。大家如果想联系你，可以在哪里找到你呢？听众能如何帮到你呢？

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: I have a handle, it's everywhere. Basically, P-A-D-D-A-Y. It's Paddy with an extra A. So, P-A-D-D-A-Y. That's everywhere. So, paddy@gmail, @Paddy. It's my handle everywhere. So, that's where you can find me. I'd love people to reach out to me, right, genuinely learn. I'd love to hear from people who think my AI talk is nonsense and it's more a crypto Web3. Or, I'd love to hear people who have alternative opinions and challenge mine. That's how I like to learn and get better. So, if people have those opinions, I'd love to hear them. I'd love to talk to them.
turns.zh: 我的账号到处都有。基本上是P-A-D-D-A-Y。Paddy多加个A。所以P-A-D-D-A-Y，到处都是。邮箱paddy@gmail，@Paddy。这些都是我的常用账号。大家可以通过这些联系到我。我希望能和大家交流，真心学习。我很乐意听到有人觉得我的AI讲座是胡说八道，觉得它更像加密货币Web3的。或者有不同观点挑战我的。这就是我学习和进步的方式。所以如果大家有不同意见，欢迎和我讨论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Be careful what you wish for. The YouTube comments are always a spicy place. We'll see what we see. Awesome, Paul. Thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 小心许愿。YouTube评论区总是很热闹。看看会怎样吧。太棒了，保罗。再次感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.speaker: Paul Adams
turns.en: Yeah, thanks Lenny. I really appreciate it.
turns.zh: 是啊，谢谢你，莱尼。我真的很感激。
